prompt: Write a novel about a teenage heroine who grows up and ends up changing the world

outline.name: The Defective Harbor
outline.description: Sixteen-year-old Mara Venn repairs a failing water pump in the Salvage Belt while concealing the emotional irregularities of her defective harbor. Her unfiltered grief, anger, and wonder make ordinary life dangerous in a society where emotional compliance is considered health. She cares for her ten-year-old brother, Eli, and argues with her skeptical friend Ivo Renn about whether the Directorate truly protects the floating city. A sudden harbor malfunction leaves Mara briefly seeing a fragment of a memory that does not belong to her: a drowned street, a protest banner, and her missing mother, Sera.

outline.name: Wreckage Field
outline.description: Sixteen-year-old Mara and Ivo search the submerged ruins beneath New Carthage for machine parts. They encounter security patrols, displaced raft families, and evidence that the upper districts receive better water and power despite official claims of equality. Mara finds an archival unit in a collapsed government building and risks arrest to retrieve it. Back home, she repairs enough of the device to hear an encrypted voice recording. The voice says that memory is not always evidence of truth, but that forgetting can be engineered. Mara recognizes Sera's voice and begins secretly studying the machine.

outline.name: A Machine That Remembers
outline.description: Mara discovers that the archival unit contains fragments of old harbor code. Her harbor reacts violently to the data, producing contradictory medical alerts and exposing flashes of suppressed memories. She hides the symptoms from neighborhood health monitors while Eli worries that his sixteen-year-old sister will be taken for stabilization. Ivo helps her access maintenance channels but warns that investigating Directorate systems could endanger them both. The recovered code references a classified project called HARBORLIGHT and a series of altered public records from the years after the great sea rise.

outline.name: The Song Under the Market
outline.description: Following a clue in the code, Mara visits an elderly dockworker who sings a forbidden version of the city's founding song. The lyrics describe evacuation ships deliberately diverted away from poor districts. Directorate officers interrupt the gathering, forcing Mara, Ivo, and Eli to flee through market tunnels. Mara learns that fragments of history survive in songs, murals, recipes, and children's games because official archives cannot be trusted. The dockworker gives her a hand-copied list of names, including Sera Venn, and tells Mara to seek the Rememberers.

outline.name: The Rememberers
outline.description: Ivo leads Mara to an underground archive hidden inside an abandoned school. There she meets Anja Quill, a former Directorate historian, and Tomas Vale, a dockworkers' organizer. The Rememberers preserve unedited memories through handmade books and mechanical recording devices. Mara distrusts their politics but shows them the archival unit. Anja confirms that HARBORLIGHT was built to regulate emotions and later expanded to edit memory. Tomas urges immediate sabotage, while Anja insists that evidence must be gathered carefully before the city is pushed into panic.

outline.name: The Official Past
outline.description: Mara compares Directorate textbooks with the forbidden songs and discovers systematic contradictions. The official history claims the first sea rise was an unavoidable natural disaster, while the hidden records show that industrial monopolies delayed flood defenses and redirected evacuation resources. Mara finds emergency votes signed by the families who now control New Carthage. She also discovers that HARBORLIGHT erased the names of thousands of protesters. Among them is Sera, whose disappearance was not listed as a storm death but as an unresolved security incident.

outline.name: The Name of Sera Venn
outline.description: Mara becomes obsessed with proving that her mother was part of the resistance. Anja explains that Sera was an engineer who helped design HARBORLIGHT before discovering its memory-editing function. Ivo challenges Mara's assumption that Sera was a hero, reminding her that abandoned children inherit the consequences of every political choice. Mara and Eli argue about their mother, and Eli admits he remembers almost nothing of her. Mara promises to find the truth without allowing the Directorate to use family grief against them.

outline.name: Relay Station Seven
outline.description: Mara, Ivo, and a young Rememberer named Pell infiltrate an old relay station beneath the Salvage Belt. They retrieve a partial technical map showing that HARBORLIGHT is integrated into medical records, employment assignments, education, food distribution, and city communications. A security drone nearly captures them, and Mara must deliberately trigger an emotional surge to confuse its predictive systems. The success makes the Rememberers see her defective harbor as a possible advantage, but Mara fears becoming valuable only because she is damaged.

outline.name: The Drowned Transit Hub
outline.description: The investigation leads into the chemically polluted foundations of the old city. Wearing improvised diving gear, Mara and Ivo enter a submerged transit hub containing a sealed memory vault. They recover Sera's recorded testimony: HARBORLIGHT cannot simply be shut down without causing neurological harm, and its compliance functions must be separated from its medical systems. Sera describes a plan to return suppressed memories gradually through local communities. The recording ends abruptly with evidence that she was discovered by Directorate agents.

outline.name: A Guardian's Offer
outline.description: Minister Cassian Or, head of the Directorate's Stability Ministry, learns that Mara has accessed HARBORLIGHT records. He publicly announces a new campaign against a supposed neurological contagion spread by terrorists. Privately, he summons Mara through a manipulated harbor message and offers to restore her harbor and protect Eli if she reveals the Rememberers' locations. Cassian admits that the old Directorate made terrible choices but argues that controlled memory is the only thing preventing civilizational collapse. Mara refuses, though she is shaken by the possibility that he may be partly right.

outline.name: The Raid on the Belt
outline.description: Security forces raid the Salvage Belt, seizing archives and arresting mechanics, teachers, and dockworkers. Mara returns home to find their room searched and Eli missing. The Directorate declares Eli a state ward because Mara has been classified as a terrorist. The raid makes the danger to Mara's family undeniable. Tomas demands retaliation against the desalination engines, while Anja warns that destroying them would kill thousands. Mara blames herself for bringing danger to her brother. Ivo proposes using his courier routes to locate the detention center, but their disagreement over methods begins to fracture their friendship.

outline.name: The Price of Compliance
outline.description: Mara surrenders to the Directorate in exchange for Eli's promised release. She is taken to an upper-district correction facility and subjected to tests designed to map her harbor's failures. Cassian shows her Eli through a controlled interview: the boy has already been given a modified harbor and struggles to remember their mother. Cassian argues that Mara's emotional instability caused the crisis and offers one final bargain—name the Rememberers and submit to correction. Mara nearly accepts when Eli recognizes her voice, then fails to recognize her face.

outline.name: The Children in the White Rooms
outline.description: While held in the correction facility, Mara discovers that many children from poor districts are being conditioned to forget hunger, displacement, and family members labeled disruptive. She befriends a frightened child whose memories have been repeatedly edited. Ivo infiltrates the facility as a Directorate courier and sees the conditioning firsthand, destroying his belief that the system is merely flawed. Mara and Ivo reconnect through coded maintenance messages. Together they plan an escape, but Mara insists that freeing only Eli would leave the other children behind.

outline.name: The Evacuation
outline.description: A storm damages the facility's platform, creating a narrow opportunity for escape. Ivo sabotages internal locks while Mara uses her harbor's contradictory signals to confuse the security network. Rather than flee alone, she broadcasts the children's location to dockworkers and market families. Ordinary citizens arrive through maintenance passages, turning the escape into a coordinated prison break. Eli is rescued but emotionally altered, and many children emerge unable to trust their own memories. The Directorate loses control of the facility, marking the first open collective victory against the regime.

outline.name: A Different Kind of Uprising
outline.description: The Rememberers debate what comes next. Tomas argues that the prison break proves the city is ready for an attack on the central tower. Mara presents Sera's alternative: release evidence gradually through trusted local channels while building systems that let people survive the transition. Anja supports her but warns that organizing communities is slower and more difficult than destroying infrastructure. Eli begins drawing fragmented images from his erased memories. Mara accepts a public role reluctantly, agreeing to coordinate archives while insisting that no single leader should own the movement.

outline.name: Memory Houses
outline.description: Over the next two years, Mara travels among the floating districts, helping establish memory houses where residents can compare personal accounts with recovered records. Each community remembers the catastrophe differently, and some stories contradict one another. Mara learns to distinguish truth from certainty without dismissing either. Ivo rebuilds courier routes between districts, while Anja trains volunteer archivists. Eli turns his frightening visions into murals that allow children to discuss loss. The movement expands from a secret network into a civic culture based on testimony, debate, and shared repair work.

outline.name: The Work of Trust
outline.description: Mara helps organize free schools, communal repair yards, and neighborhood councils. The movement wins small victories by forcing the Directorate to share food and energy reserves. Mara struggles with exhaustion and with people who treat her as a symbol rather than a person. Tomas criticizes her refusal to authorize attacks, while Anja warns that compromise can become another form of obedience. Mara and Ivo's friendship deepens into love, but both recognize that their work leaves little room for a private future. Mara learns that changing the world requires patient administration as much as courage.

outline.name: The Counterhistory
outline.description: Cassian responds with a sophisticated propaganda campaign. The Directorate releases edited archives that admit minor abuses while claiming the founding families prevented an even greater disaster. It accuses Mara of manipulating grief and using children as political weapons. Some upper-district residents begin attending public debates, while others demand harsher security. Mara discovers that several Rememberer testimonies were also exaggerated, forcing her to publicly correct allies and risk weakening the movement. Her decision earns trust from some citizens and anger from those who believe victory requires a simple story.

outline.name: The Blackout Riot
outline.description: A coordinated Directorate blackout cuts power and water to several lower districts. Panic spreads, and a confrontation in the upper districts becomes a riot that kills hundreds. Cassian blames Mara and declares that all harbors will soon enter permanent compliance mode. Tomas demands the destruction of the central desalination controls, and many young activists support him. Mara opposes the plan but cannot offer immediate protection to starving families. The movement fractures between negotiators, saboteurs, and those who want to seize the tower, while Mara realizes that truth without practical preparation can become another instrument of violence.

outline.name: Sera's Last Instruction
outline.description: Mara returns to the submerged transit hub with Eli and Ivo to search for the missing portion of Sera's plan. They find a final recording explaining how to separate HARBORLIGHT's medical protections from its obedience protocols during the annual synchronization. Sera admits she could not save everyone and asks whoever finds the recording to build safeguards against any future authority controlling memory. She confirms that she was captured and likely killed, but leaves technical instructions and a warning: no broadcast should occur unless communities are ready to care for one another afterward. Mara chooses preparation over revenge.

outline.name: The Long Campaign
outline.description: Five more years pass as Mara and the movement build a decentralized civic network. Neighborhood assemblies practice emergency distribution, independent medical care, and collective archiving. Tomas leads strikes rather than sabotage, winning concessions while preserving essential infrastructure. Ivo coordinates couriers and schools. Eli becomes a public artist whose murals restore erased names to walls across the city. Mara becomes a skilled organizer and speaker but repeatedly rejects demands that she become the movement's permanent leader. Cassian prepares a final synchronization meant to lock every harbor into compliance.

outline.name: The Festival of Renewal
outline.description: At thirty, Mara learns that the Directorate will synchronize every harbor during the Festival of Renewal, creating the only opportunity to reach the entire city at once. The movement prepares thousands of local archive stations, medical teams, food depots, and discussion circles. The plan is dangerous: releasing suppressed memories may trigger neurological distress, violence, or infrastructure failure. Mara and Ivo argue over whether the people can truly consent under such pressure. Mara decides that the broadcast must include not only the crimes of the past but also practical instructions and a promise that no authority will control the next story.

outline.name: The Broadcast
outline.description: As the Festival begins, Mara, Ivo, Anja, Tomas, and their allies seize the central relay beneath New Carthage. Cassian confronts Mara and insists that he is preventing a second collapse. Mara acknowledges the genuine danger but rejects the idea that safety can be built on permanent infantilization. She transmits the complete archive: the Directorate's climate crimes, the erased names, Sera's testimony, and generations of resistance. Alongside the history, she broadcasts instructions for preserving medical functions, disabling compliance protocols, and forming neighborhood assemblies. The city receives its buried past all at once.

outline.name: When the Harbors Open
outline.description: The broadcast produces confusion, grief, and isolated violence, but the preparation of the civic network prevents total collapse. Teachers guide discussions, medics treat harbor-related trauma, and local councils distribute food and power. Harbor technicians remove obedience protocols district by district. Upper-district residents open private reservoirs, dockworkers refuse military orders, and soldiers abandon their posts after seeing unedited memories of their families' losses. Cassian loses control of the Directorate and disappears into the submerged ruins. Mara refuses to claim personal victory, directing the movement to protect even former officials from mob justice.

outline.name: Nothing Belongs to One Voice
outline.description: Several years later, New Carthage is governed by a federated civic assembly with public archives that no authority can secretly alter. Mara is an elected archivist and mother, while Ivo coordinates schools and repair cooperatives and Eli teaches visual history. The new society remains imperfect: resources are contested, old prejudices persist, and some citizens still long for the certainty of the Directorate. Mara helps children study the catastrophe alongside the movement's mistakes and the failures of the new government. She reflects on Sera's legacy and understands that the world changed not because one hero owned the truth, but because ordinary people learned to preserve, question, and act on it together.

chapters.name: The Defective Harbor
chapters.content:
## The Defective Harbor

The pump began screaming before dawn.

Mara Venn heard it through three walls of patched metal, beneath the cough of the neighbors’ heater and the slap of waves against the Salvage Belt. It was a thin, rising shriek, like a kettle discovering pain. She opened her eyes in the dark and counted the seconds between each shudder.

Four. Four. Three. Four.

“Go back to sleep,” Eli murmured from the other cot.

“I wasn’t awake.”

“You’re talking.”

“So are you.”

At the foot of Mara’s cot, her harbor blinked a pale blue warning across the inside of her wrist.

**AFFECTIVE DEVIATION: ELEVATED.**

The message faded, then returned in green.

**AFFECTIVE DEVIATION: WITHIN ACCEPTABLE RANGE.**

Mara pulled her sleeve over it.

Their room was a cargo container welded into the western rim of New Carthage, where the city’s old freight platforms had been joined to fishing pontoons, roof gardens, and whatever else would float. Rain ticked on the corrugated roof. The air smelled of salt, hot wiring, and the algae paste Eli had spilled yesterday.

The pump screamed again.

Mara sat up.

“If it stops,” Eli said, “we don’t have water.”

“If it stops, everyone on this row doesn’t have water.”

“That’s worse.”

“It’s more motivating.”

She dressed by touch: work trousers, insulated boots, the gray utility coat whose elbows had been patched with sailcloth. Eli watched from beneath his blanket, all eyes and hair, ten years old and trying to look older whenever she left the room.

“Don’t open the door for anyone,” she said.

“What if it’s a monitor?”

“Especially then.”

“What if it’s Ivo?”

“He’ll pick the lock and complain about the lock.”

“I like when he complains.”

“You like when he brings sweetbread.”

“I can like two things.”

Mara paused with her hand on the latch. The ordinary warmth of the exchange moved through her too quickly, too brightly. Her chest tightened. For one dangerous instant she wanted to laugh, to seize Eli and spin him around the room until both of them fell dizzy onto the floor.

Her harbor flashed red beneath her sleeve.

**AFFECTIVE DEVIATION: ACUTE. SEEK CALMING GUIDANCE.**

She pressed two fingers against the warning until the skin hurt.

“Flat voice,” she reminded herself.

Eli’s face closed a little. “I know.”

She hated that he knew.

Outside, the Salvage Belt hung beneath the brighter districts like a second thought. New Carthage was a floating city only if one looked from far away. Up close, it was a thousand compromises: rusted pontoons under apartment towers, desalination pipes crossing alleys overhead, gardens growing in oil drums, walkways that flexed with every tide. Above the Belt, the upper rings shone pearl-white in the dawn. Their windows reflected the rising sun. Down here, the sun arrived diluted through steam and smoke.

The pump station crouched at the end of Pier Nine, surrounded by coils of hose and crates marked PROPERTY OF THE DIRECTORATE. Mara ducked under the chain barrier. The station’s access panel had been pried open and resealed so many times that it resembled a metal scab.

Ivo Renn was already inside.

He sat on the pump housing with a wrench across his knees, long legs dangling, dark hair wet from the rain. “You’re late.”

“It’s before dawn.”

“That’s when late is easiest.”

“You came without a sweetbread.”

“I came with superior moral purpose.”

“Can it be exchanged for breakfast?”

“Not in this economy.”

The pump shrieked. Ivo slid down and lifted the inspection plate. Brown water trembled in the pipes.

Mara crouched beside him. “Pressure valve’s sticking.”

“Already cleaned it.”

“Then you cleaned the wrong part.”

“I cleaned the part that looked dirty.”

“That explains most of your life.”

He gave her a sideways smile, but his eyes went to her covered wrist. “Your harbor report?”

“Quiet.”

“Quiet means you’re lying.”

“Quiet means I’m working.”

Every resident carried a harbor: a small implant threaded into the nervous system during childhood, designed to regulate stress, identify illness, and keep the city’s population emotionally synchronized. The Directorate called it public health. School lessons called it the reason New Carthage had survived the sea rise. The monitors called it whenever they entered a room: a harbor was safe when its signals were smooth.

Mara’s had never been smooth.

She loosened the valve casing. The metal was hot despite the cold morning. Ivo held the lamp while she worked.

“Upper ring got water all night,” he said.

“Good for them.”

“Three uninterrupted hours.”

She looked up. “How do you know?”

“My cousin works freight elevators. The pressure logs pass through his terminal.”

“Pressure logs aren’t district gossip.”

“Everything is district gossip if people are thirsty.”

Mara scraped mineral crust from the valve. “The Directorate says rationing is equal.”

“The Directorate says lots of things.”

“And you believe none of them?”

“I believe water runs downhill.”

“This city floats.”

“Exactly. So someone is pumping it uphill.”

The valve came free with a crack. A spray struck Mara across the cheek. She flinched, and the harbor under her sleeve stuttered.

**THREAT RESPONSE:—**

The letters dissolved into a string of symbols.

Mara swallowed. “Hand me the blue seal.”

Ivo didn’t move. “That was a warning.”

“It’s a pump.”

“It’s your wrist.”

“Blue seal, Ivo.”

He handed it over. His fingers brushed hers. The contact was brief, but concern rose from him so plainly that she felt it as if it were her own. His worry became heat behind her ribs. Her anger followed, sharp and immediate—not at him, not exactly, but at the harbor for making every feeling public to a machine that could report it.

The monitor above the door woke.

**CITIZEN VENN, MARA. PLEASE MAINTAIN EMOTIONAL STEADINESS.**

Ivo’s jaw tightened. “It’s not even connected to the district net.”

“Everything is connected to the district net.”

“Then why does it need to tell you how to feel?”

“Because apparently I’m bad at it.”

The pump gave a violent lurch. The floor tilted beneath them. Outside, someone shouted as the pier rolled against its anchors.

Mara thrust the seal into place and gripped the housing. The pump’s vibration traveled up through her bones. For a moment the station vanished behind a pressure of sound: water forced through old pipes, voices layered under it, a thousand people speaking at once.

Then she saw a street.

Not Pier Nine. Not any street in New Carthage now.

Buildings rose on either side, their lower windows black with seawater. A red banner snapped between two lamp posts. The words were blurred, but she could make out **WE WERE PROMISED**. People stood knee-deep in the flood, faces turned toward a line of armored boats.

A woman in a yellow raincoat lifted both hands.

Sera.

Mara knew the slope of her shoulders, the dark braid plastered to her neck. Her mother was younger than Mara remembered and older than any photograph they owned. She was shouting something. The sound came through the pump as a broken metallic pulse.

Behind Sera, water rushed through a shattered transit entrance.

A hand seized her arm.

Sera turned. Her mouth formed Mara’s name.

The vision broke.

Mara came back on her knees, clutching the pump housing. Ivo was shouting. The warning monitor had gone black. Water hammered the pipes, then settled into a steady low thrum.

“Mara.” He caught her shoulder. “Mara, look at me.”

She looked at him.

His face was frightened. That frightened her more.

“Did you fall?”

“No.”

“You were gone.”

“I was here.”

“You said something.”

“What?”

He hesitated. “You said, ‘Don’t take her.’”

The station smelled of rust and brine. Mara’s cheek was cold where the spray had dried.

“Pump’s fixed,” she said.

Ivo stared at her. “That isn’t what I asked.”

The access door rattled. Footsteps crossed the pier. A monitor voice announced that a district health inspection was in progress.

Mara stood too quickly. The room tilted again, though nothing showed on her wrist now. She gathered the tools and shoved them into her case.

“Inspection,” Ivo said. “You should report the malfunction.”

“To whom?”

“The maintenance office.”

“They’ll replace the pump with one that fails louder.”

“They’ll scan you.”

“I know.”

A fist struck the door.

“Citizen Venn,” called a calm voice. “Open for wellness verification.”

Mara looked at Ivo. He had gone pale beneath his brown skin. Skepticism was easy in alleys and market stalls. It became something else when boots waited outside.

“Back hatch,” he whispered.

“There’s no back hatch.”

“There is if you dislike the front one enough.”

He kicked a panel below the pressure gauges. It folded inward, revealing a maintenance crawlspace barely wide enough for a child.

Mara thought of Eli alone in the room. She thought of Sera in the drowned street, turning toward her through impossible water.

The door shook under another blow.

“Go,” Ivo said.

Mara slid into the crawlspace. Before following, he reached for the panel, then stopped.

“What?” she whispered.

“Your harbor.”

She pulled back her sleeve. The skin was marked with a faint blue pulse.

**AFFECTIVE DEVIATION: UNRESOLVED.**

Ivo read it. “That’s not a diagnosis.”

“No.”

“It sounds like a question.”

The door began to open.

Mara crawled into darkness, carrying the wrench, the blue seal, and a memory that did not belong to her. Behind her, Ivo slammed the panel shut. Above the pipes, the inspector called her name with patient certainty.

Somewhere beyond the walls, the repaired pump began to turn.

Its rhythm followed her all the way home.

set.name: Mara Venn
set.description: At the end of the chapter, Mara is in the maintenance passages on her way home to the Salvage Belt, carrying her wrench, blue seal, and tool case. She is sixteen, responsible for ten-year-old Eli, and wants to keep him safe while repairing essential machinery and understanding why her harbor malfunctions. She distrusts Directorate health surveillance and argues that its claims of equal protection are false, but still has no proof. Her defective harbor produces contradictory alerts and an unresolved status; it has just shown her a memory of a drowned street, a protest banner, and her missing mother Sera. She is frightened, angry at the loss of control, and determined to conceal the event from inspectors. She has a close, argumentative friendship with Ivo Renn, who has just helped her escape and now knows she saw something impossible. She possesses her harbor implant, work clothes, tools, and the unexplained memory fragment.

set.name: Eli Venn
set.description: Eli is ten and waiting alone in the Venn cargo-container home in the Salvage Belt after Mara left to repair the pump. He depends on Mara for care and understands that Directorate monitors are dangerous, though he tries to hide his fear with jokes. He is attached to Mara and likes Ivo, especially when Ivo brings sweetbread. He does not know about Mara's vision or its connection to their missing mother. His current condition is physically safe but anxious about Mara's absence and the district's water failure.

set.name: Ivo Renn
set.description: Ivo is at or just beyond the concealed maintenance route leading away from Pier Nine after helping Mara evade a Directorate wellness inspection. He is Mara's skeptical, quick-witted friend and a mechanic/courier-minded resident with access to pressure-log gossip through his cousin's freight-elevator work. He questions the Directorate's claim that water rationing is equal and now knows Mara's harbor issued abnormal alerts and that she experienced a memory involving Sera, making him concerned and more directly entangled. He carries or has access to his wrench and work gear; emotionally he is frightened but protective and still inclined to investigate rather than accept official explanations.

set.name: Sera Venn
set.description: Sera Venn is Mara and Eli's missing mother; her present whereabouts are unknown. In Mara's harbor-induced fragment, Sera appeared younger, wearing a yellow raincoat, standing knee-deep in floodwater on a drowned street beneath a red protest banner, shouting as armored boats approached and turning as if calling Mara's name. Mara has no confirmed explanation for whether this was memory, recorded data, or hallucination.
Mara repaired the failing Pier Nine water pump just before a Directorate wellness inspection arrived.
A harbor malfunction gave Mara a vivid fragment of an unfamiliar drowned street where she saw Sera Venn holding a protest banner and calling Mara's name.
Ivo helped Mara escape the pump station through a concealed maintenance crawlspace when inspectors arrived.
Mara must keep the unresolved harbor malfunction and the vision of Sera hidden from district health inspectors while continuing to care for Eli.
Ivo now knows Mara experienced an impossible memory and must decide whether to help her evade Directorate scrutiny.

chapters.name: Wreckage Field
chapters.content:
## Chapter 1: Wreckage Field

By dawn, the water below New Carthage had turned the color of old coins.

Mara leaned over the rail of the salvage skiff and watched plastic weed curl around the pilings. The city floated above her in layers: the bright upper rings with their glass gardens and polished wind vanes, the middle districts stacked from old ferry decks, and beneath them the drowned city, where streets and buildings slept under twelve meters of green-black water.

Ivo tightened the strap of his borrowed breathing mask. “You’re staring again.”

“I’m checking the current.”

“The current is moving left. You’ve been checking it since we left.”

Mara looked at him. His dark hair was tied back with copper wire, and a smear of machine grease crossed his cheek. He had brought two sacks, one pry bar, and the expression of someone who had already decided their plan was stupid but intended to help anyway.

“You said Pier Nine’s pump needs a pressure coil,” she told him. “If I don’t find one, the district gets half-rationed again tonight.”

“Half-rationed according to the district board.”

“According to the pump.”

“Pumps don’t write the notices.”

She heard the warning beneath the joke. Ivo had been saying things like that for months, quietly, as if the walls might repeat him. The Directorate’s notices claimed every district received the same allotment of water and current, adjusted only for population and emergency need. Yet the Salvage Belt’s taps coughed brown water while the upper rings lit their gardens through the night.

Mara had no proof. Proof was a luxury that required time, dry paper, and somewhere safe to keep it.

She checked the seal on her work jacket and stepped into the water.

The cold struck through the suit at once. Her harbor tightened behind her left ear, registering temperature, pressure, oxygen, and the familiar uncertainty that had followed her since childhood.

HEALTH STATUS: STABLE.

A breath later, another line appeared.

HEALTH STATUS: UNRESOLVED.

Mara swallowed. The water muffled the city until all she could hear was the soft hiss of her mask. Ivo descended beside her, his lamp swinging across the submerged ruins.

They passed the roof of a tram station, its old sign wavering in the current. Fish nested in the broken letters. Beyond it stood the government quarter, or what remained of it: towers split open by the sea rise, offices filled with silt, bridges descending into darkness like snapped ribs.

A family lived inside the shell of a delivery barge nearby. Their raft was made from doors, foam tanks, and a bright red children’s pool. A woman in a patched pressure suit watched Mara and Ivo approach. Two boys clung to the raft’s side, their faces pale behind fogged masks.

“Spare filter?” the woman asked through the water speaker.

Ivo shook his head. “Only parts.”

“Parts become filters.”

Mara stopped. The woman’s gauge showed a warning stripe. Their shelter’s battery was nearly dead, and the children’s masks were homemade. Mara had one spare charcoal cartridge in her tool case, meant for Eli’s cough if it worsened.

She looked at the boys. One was no older than Eli.

Ivo caught her wrist. “Mara.”

“I know.”

She unclipped the cartridge and passed it over. The woman stared at it, then pressed both hands together in thanks.

When they swam on, Ivo said, “That was for Eli.”

“I know.”

“You can’t repair the whole city one cartridge at a time.”

“No. But I can repair one family’s air.”

The wreckage field opened beneath them. Once, this had been a plaza. Marble statues lay on their sides. Buses rested nose-down in the silt. The current had stripped everything bright from the old world except warning paint and advertisements for things no one manufactured anymore.

Mara found the first pressure coil inside a maintenance cabinet. It was corroded, but the inner filament looked intact. She tucked it into her sack and marked the cabinet with a strip of blue tape.

Then a white beam swept across the ruins.

SECURITY PATROL.

The message appeared in Mara’s vision, followed by an instruction to remain still and present identification. Her harbor repeated it in three contradictory tones: calm, urgent, and almost curious.

Ivo pointed toward the collapsed courthouse. They kicked through a doorway and flattened themselves beneath a fallen slab. Above them, a patrol skimmer glided through the water, its drone lamps searching windows and stairwells. Directorate security officially came down only to protect salvage crews from unstable structures. Everyone knew they also checked who was taking what, and for whom.

A voice crackled through the water.

“Unauthorized descent detected. Salvage permits will be verified.”

Ivo’s hand found Mara’s in the dark. His fingers were cold.

The skimmer paused outside. Mara could see the blue band of its inspection light inching over the floor. In her harbor, a pulse began behind her ear.

COMPLIANCE RESPONSE AVAILABLE.

She held her breath until the light moved away. The skimmer continued toward the raft family.

“Come on,” Ivo whispered.

They pushed deeper into the courthouse.

The building had fallen sideways, making its corridors into sloping tunnels. Mara’s lamp passed over rows of drowned desks and a wall painted with the Directorate’s founding oath. Most of the lettering had peeled away. Underneath, someone had scratched a different sentence into the plaster:

WE WERE HERE.

At the end of the corridor, a metal door stood half-buried in silt. The seal bore an emblem Mara recognized from old municipal pumps: a circle crossed by three lines. Ivo wedged the pry bar into the gap.

“Government archive,” he said.

“Then leave it.”

“Government archives have copper.”

He pulled. The door groaned, and a cloud of black silt rolled over them. Inside was a narrow room packed with dead consoles. One unit remained mounted beneath a desk, protected by a casing of thick gray polymer. Its indicator blinked once when Mara’s lamp passed over it.

Her harbor flared.

UNKNOWN DEVICE.

Then:

FAMILIAR SIGNAL.

Mara reached toward it.

Ivo caught her arm. “No.”

“I’m not touching it.”

“You’re looking at it like it called your name.”

The patrol beam flashed across the broken courthouse above them. A dull impact followed. The security team was searching the building.

Mara saw the unit’s small blue seal and thought of the vision from Pier Nine: Sera in floodwater, turning beneath a red banner. Not a dream. Not exactly. The same impossible pressure gathered behind her eyes.

“Ivo,” she said, “we take it.”

“That is not a machine part.”

“No.”

“Then what is it?”

“I don’t know.”

The answer frightened him. It frightened her more.

He still drew the pry bar from his belt. Together they worked the casing loose. The bolts had fused, and Mara had to use her wrench with both hands. Her pulse battered the harbor implant. Alerts crowded her vision until the room broke into overlapping outlines.

PRESERVE MEDICAL STABILITY.

REPORT ANOMALOUS COGNITIVE RESPONSE.

DO NOT REPORT.

The last instruction vanished so quickly she wondered whether she had imagined it.

The casing came free. The archival unit was heavier than it looked, dense with old storage plates and sealed ports. Mara tucked it under her jacket.

A drone’s metal legs clicked over the floor above.

Ivo pointed toward a drainage shaft. They shoved themselves through just as the patrol entered the room. Mara’s shoulder struck concrete. Her tool case snagged. She let it go, then reached back and seized it by the handle.

“Mara!”

She kicked into the shaft. Ivo followed. Behind them, a security drone fired a scanning pulse. It passed through Mara’s body like a second heartbeat.

Her vision filled with a street under water.

Sera wore a yellow raincoat. She stood knee-deep in floodwater beneath a red banner. Armored boats moved between the buildings. Sera shouted something, and Mara—small, impossibly small—stood on a doorstep holding a tin cup.

Then Sera turned.

Not toward the boats. Toward Mara.

Her mouth formed a name.

The vision snapped shut.

Mara struck the bottom of the shaft and landed on her knees. Ivo grabbed her shoulders.

“What did you see?”

She could not answer. Water streamed from her mask. Her harbor displayed no alert at all.

They escaped through a maintenance culvert and surfaced two streets from the salvage skiff. By the time they reached it, the patrol had moved on. The raft family’s lamps were dark, but the children were still alive, huddled beneath the red pool.

Ivo started the skiff’s engine. “You’re going to tell me.”

Mara held the archival unit between her boots. “It may be nothing.”

“You saw her.”

The city’s upper rings shone ahead, reflected in the polluted water. Mara thought of Eli waiting in their cargo container with the last clean cup of water.

“I saw something that looked like my mother,” she said.

Ivo’s jaw tightened. “That is not the same as nothing.”

At home, Eli was asleep beside the heater, one hand curled around Mara’s blue seal as if he had been waiting for her to return. She covered him with a blanket and carried the unit to the workbench.

For three hours she opened its casing, cleaned contacts, and rebuilt a power bridge from the dead pump’s discarded regulator. The device resisted every ordinary connection. When she finally pressed the blue seal into its port, the room lights flickered.

A voice emerged through static.

“—if you are hearing this, memory is not always evidence of truth.”

Mara stopped breathing.

The recording crackled, distorted by age and encryption.

“Memory can be wounded. It can be borrowed. It can be made to resemble obedience. But forgetting can be engineered. Do not confuse the absence of a memory with the absence of an event.”

Eli stirred in his sleep.

Mara turned the volume lower, though the voice had already entered every part of her.

Sera.

Older than in the vision, perhaps. Tired. Certain. Her mother’s voice, saying words no official system would permit.

The recording dissolved into a sequence of tones. A lock symbol appeared on the unit’s cracked screen, followed by a line of unfamiliar code.

Mara copied it into the margin of an old repair manual. Then she disconnected the power and wrapped the archival unit in a pair of Eli’s winter socks.

At the doorway, she looked back at the machine.

The harbor behind her ear whispered two different diagnoses.

HEALTH STATUS: STABLE.

HEALTH STATUS: UNRESOLVED.

Mara sat beside Eli until dawn, one hand on his shoulder and the other resting on the hidden unit. She had spent her life repairing things that failed in public. This would have to remain broken in secret, at least until she understood what it remembered—and what someone had tried to make the city forget.

set.name: Mara Venn
set.description: Mara is sixteen and back in the Venn cargo-container home in the Salvage Belt, sitting beside sleeping Eli after secretly repairing and activating a recovered archival unit. She wants to protect Eli, keep her harbor malfunction and impossible visions hidden from Directorate inspectors, understand the machine, and learn whether the recording in Sera's recognizable voice is genuine. She now knows the submerged ruins and raft families suffer poor air, water, and power while upper districts shine, though she has no formal proof. She possesses her harbor implant, work clothes, wrench and tools, the blue seal, the hidden archival unit wrapped in Eli's socks, and a copied encrypted code. She is frightened, exhausted, emotionally shaken by hearing Sera, and determined to investigate without exposing Eli.

set.name: Eli Venn
set.description: Eli is ten and asleep in the Venn cargo-container home in the Salvage Belt after waiting anxiously for Mara's return. He depends on Mara, likes Ivo, and does not know about the archival unit, Sera's recording, or Mara's vision. He is physically safe but vulnerable, with the household's water and resources still precarious; he is sleeping beside the heater while Mara keeps watch.

set.name: Ivo Renn
set.description: Ivo is sixteen and has returned with Mara to the Venn home after their submerged search. He is Mara's close, argumentative friend, a mechanic and courier-minded resident with a skeptical view of Directorate claims. He helped search the wreckage field, aided Mara in evading a security patrol, and knows she saw something resembling Sera and recovered an unexplained archival unit. He is frightened but protective and likely to press Mara for answers. He possesses his work gear and wrench and remains directly entangled in the investigation.

set.name: Sera Venn
set.description: Sera Venn remains missing, with her whereabouts and fate unknown. Mara has now heard a damaged encrypted recording in a voice she recognizes as Sera's, warning that memory is not always evidence of truth and that forgetting can be engineered. This gives Mara stronger reason to investigate but does not confirm when or where the recording was made. Sera's earlier appearance in Mara's harbor-induced fragment remains unresolved.

Mara and Ivo searched the submerged ruins beneath New Carthage, aided a displaced raft family with Mara's spare air filter, and found evidence of unequal conditions beneath the Directorate's equality claims.
Mara and Ivo recovered a sealed archival unit bearing a municipal blue seal from a collapsed government building while evading a Directorate security patrol.
Mara repaired the archival unit enough to hear an encrypted recording in Sera Venn's recognizable voice warning that forgetting can be engineered, then hid the unit at home.
Mara copied an unfamiliar encrypted code from the archival unit and began secretly studying the machine while Eli slept.
Mara must secretly study the recovered archival unit and decipher its encrypted code without alerting Directorate health inspectors or endangering Eli.
Mara must investigate the recording's warning that forgetting can be engineered and determine how the archival unit is connected to Sera and the city's harbor systems.

chapters.name: A Machine That Remembers
chapters.content:
## Chapter 2: A Machine That Remembers

The machine disliked being hidden.

Mara discovered this before breakfast, when Eli was still asleep and the Salvage Belt’s pipes were knocking themselves awake. The archival unit lay on the workbench beneath a stack of broken pressure gauges, wrapped in Eli’s winter socks. Every few seconds, a blue light pulsed through the wool.

She lifted one sock. The unit’s casing was dull gray, its municipal seal scratched but intact. It had no visible power cell. Mara had fed it current from the pump regulator and then disconnected it, yet it continued to glow as if remembering the electricity.

“Stop that,” she whispered.

The harbor behind her left ear answered.

DEVICE: INACTIVE.

A second message slid beneath it.

DEVICE: LISTENING.

Mara dropped the sock.

Across the room, Eli turned on his mattress. Their cargo container had once been a shipping box, and the thin walls carried every sound from the Belt: gulls fighting over fish skin, a winch squealing, someone coughing in the next unit. If the health monitors heard her speaking to a machine, they would call it stress behavior. If they saw the alerts in her vision, they would call it evidence.

She pulled the unit toward her and opened the casing again.

Inside, the storage plates were arranged around a narrow copper spine. Not a standard archive. Standard archives stored documents, permits, old entertainment, approved family histories. This had channels branching like veins, some cut cleanly and resealed with black resin. A row of contact points bore tiny stamped letters.

HARBOR.

Mara copied the word into her repair manual, then the symbols beside it. The copied code from the night before looked less like a lock now than a fragment of a conversation. Several instructions repeated in old harbor syntax: receive, compare, correct, suppress.

She knew those terms from pump controllers. A harbor measured water pressure, oxygen, temperature. It compared the readings with safe limits and corrected what it could. Suppression was not a mechanical word. It belonged to alarms, reports, and people who told you not to mention what everyone had seen.

She connected a thin probe to the first contact.

The room vanished.

For one breath Mara stood in a white corridor with no windows. A child sat on the floor, knees pulled to her chest. Someone was singing behind a sealed door. The child looked up, and Mara saw her own face—not sixteen, but six, wet hair plastered to her forehead.

Then the vision broke apart into numbers.

HEART RATE: 142.

HEART RATE: 68.

COGNITIVE DISTRESS: CRITICAL.

COGNITIVE DISTRESS: ACCEPTABLE.

She tore the probe free and struck the workbench. The harbor tightened painfully behind her ear.

“Assist,” she gasped. “Assist, assist—”

MEDICAL STABILITY PRESERVED.

NEUROLOGICAL IRREGULARITY DETECTED.

REPORT TO DISTRICT HEALTH.

DO NOT REPORT.

The last message appeared in the same pale blue as the unit’s light. Mara stared until all four alerts blurred together.

Eli sat up. “Mara?”

She shoved the unit under the gauges. “Go back to sleep.”

“You’re shaking.”

“I’m cold.”

“It isn’t cold.”

He was ten, not stupid. Eli had learned to read the difference between a failing heater and a failing person. Mara reached for the blanket and pulled it around her shoulders before he could see the tremor in her hands.

A tone sounded outside.

The neighborhood health monitors made their rounds at seven. Every household was supposed to present its harbor status through the wall terminal. The system recorded sleep, nutrition, emotional compliance, and implant stability. The Directorate called it preventive care. In the Belt, people called it the knock before removal.

Eli’s face changed. “Is it them?”

“Probably.”

“If they take you, who fixes the water?”

Mara looked at him. “They aren’t taking me.”

“But your harbor—”

“It’s fine.”

The lie came too quickly. Eli noticed.

Another tone, followed by a pleasant automated voice. “Venn residence. Routine wellness confirmation. Please open your terminal.”

Mara slid the archival unit into the cavity beneath the workbench and dropped a tray of washers over it. Then she pressed two fingers behind her ear, willing the harbor to present its simplest report.

STABLE.

UNRESOLVED.

She chose stable. The terminal blinked green.

“Confirmation transmitted,” it said.

A small panel beside the door opened. A neighborhood monitor’s lens glinted through the gap. “Mara Venn, are you experiencing unusual sensory events, intrusive recollections, or emotional volatility?”

“No.”

Eli looked at her.

The lens adjusted. “Please answer without hesitation.”

“No.”

“Your harbor registered a fluctuation at 04:12.”

“Pump noise.”

“Were you operating machinery?”

“Dreaming.”

The monitor paused. “Dream content can indicate early instability. A stabilization appointment is available this afternoon.”

“I have work.”

“Work accommodations can be arranged.”

Eli made a small sound behind her. Mara felt anger rise, hot and immediate, followed by the harbor’s attempt to flatten it.

COMPLIANCE RESPONSE AVAILABLE.

She smiled at the lens. “I’ll request an appointment if I need one.”

The panel closed. The footsteps outside moved on.

Eli waited until the next household’s door opened. “What is stabilization?”

“Medicine.”

“Does it make people better?”

“It makes them easier to monitor.”

She had not meant to say it. Eli’s eyes widened.

Mara knelt beside him. “Listen to me. If anyone asks, my harbor is stable. If you see me get dizzy, you tell me to sit down. You don’t tell a monitor.”

“Because they’ll take you.”

“Because they’ll ask questions we don’t want to answer yet.”

“About the machine?”

Mara went still.

Eli pointed at the workbench. “You’ve been hiding it badly.”

Despite herself, she laughed once. It hurt behind her eyes.

“I need to understand it,” she said.

“Then understand it faster.”

By midday, Ivo arrived carrying a coil of wire and two cups of bitter algae tea. He entered without knocking, as usual, then stopped when he saw Mara’s face.

“You look like the terminal tried to eat you.”

“It almost did.”

Eli moved from the table. “She says she’s fine.”

Ivo glanced at Mara. “That means she isn’t.”

Mara showed him the unit.

He did not touch it. “You brought government property into your home.”

“Municipal property.”

“That distinction has gotten people arrested.”

She unfolded the repair manual. “The code is old harbor syntax. Look.”

Ivo leaned over the page. He knew more about city maintenance channels than any mechanic his age should have. His courier work took him through service corridors, relay cupboards, and forgotten terminals where official maps disagreed with the walls.

“These symbols aren’t from pump systems,” he said. “They’re routing commands.”

“To where?”

“Everywhere, maybe.”

He connected his wire to the unit’s exposed contacts, then clipped the other end to a maintenance port beneath Mara’s workbench. The port had been dead for years, but Ivo replaced its fuse and coaxed it into a weak signal.

The unit woke.

A list unfolded across its screen, most of it corrupted.

PUBLIC RECORD—AMENDED.

CIVIC RESPONSE—AMENDED.

CASUALTY INDEX—AMENDED.

HARBORLIGHT—ACCESS RESTRICTED.

Mara read the word twice.

“What is Harborlight?” Eli asked.

“Nothing you need to worry about,” Ivo said.

The unit emitted a burst of static. Mara’s vision filled with images.

A harbor tower glowing red above a flooded district. Rows of people sitting beneath medical lamps. A woman’s hand writing names on a paper wall, then stopping as the names faded. Sera’s yellow sleeve. A door closing.

Mara cried out and fell against the bench.

The harbor screamed in silent colors.

NEUROLOGICAL FAILURE.

MEDICAL STABILITY PRESERVED.

MEMORY CONFLICT: SOURCE UNVERIFIED.

MEMORY CONFLICT: SOURCE AUTHENTIC.

Ivo ripped the wire free. The images vanished, but the pain remained.

“Mara.”

She pressed her palm to the floor. “Don’t call anyone.”

“I wasn’t going to.”

“Not even if I stop answering.”

Eli crouched beside her, frightened. “Should I get water?”

“Later.” Mara forced herself upright. “I’m here.”

Ivo’s anger arrived after his fear. “This is not a puzzle. It is inside your head.”

“It was inside the machine first.”

“That doesn’t make it safer.”

“No. It makes it evidence.”

He looked toward the door, where the health monitor’s lens had been. “We can access the maintenance channels from the old pump network. But if this unit is tied to Directorate systems, the connection may leave a trace.”

“Then don’t connect.”

“You just said it was evidence.”

“I said I need to know what it is.”

“And I’m saying knowledge has a price.”

Mara met his eyes. “You helped me steal it.”

“I helped you survive a patrol. There’s a difference.”

For a moment, neither spoke. Outside, a barge horn groaned across the water. The sound became, in Mara’s mind, the low note of an alarm.

Ivo exhaled and bent over the manual again. “There’s a maintenance mirror beneath the old school terminal. It won’t route through the district health system. We can read the unit without broadcasting a request.”

“Can?”

“Maybe.”

“Then we go tonight.”

He pointed at her. “One trace, one security ping, and we stop. No heroics. No more visions if you can help it.”

“I don’t choose them.”

“That’s what worries me.”

The unit’s screen flickered one final time. Beneath HARBORLIGHT, a line of text resolved from the corruption:

PROJECT FUNCTION: EMOTIONAL REGULATION.

PUBLIC RECORDS ALTERED: YEARS 1–7 AFTER SEA RISE.

Mara felt the room tilt. The great sea rise belonged to every official lesson, every memorial, every ration calculation. It was the beginning of the city’s history. Everyone knew what had happened.

Or everyone knew what they had been permitted to remember.

Eli took her hand. “Mara?”

She closed her fingers around his. The harbor continued to issue its impossible verdicts, one over the other, as if two authorities were fighting for the same space inside her.

STABLE.

UNRESOLVED.

She looked at Ivo. “Tonight, we find the maintenance mirror.”

He nodded, though he did not look relieved.

Under the workbench, the archival unit pulsed like a second heart. Somewhere in the buried machinery of New Carthage, something called HARBORLIGHT was still awake. It had regulated feelings, altered records, and perhaps reached into the minds of children.

Mara did not know whether the machine remembered the truth.

But it remembered that someone had tried to erase it.

set.name: Mara Venn
set.description: Mara is sixteen and in the Venn cargo-container home in the Salvage Belt, with the archival unit hidden beneath her workbench. She is determined to understand the machine, HARBORLIGHT, and the altered records while protecting ten-year-old Eli and concealing her harbor's contradictory alerts and visions from Directorate health monitors. She knows the unit contains old harbor routing code and references HARBORLIGHT's emotional-regulation function and public-record alterations during years 1–7 after the sea rise. Her harbor reacts violently to the unit, producing conflicting diagnoses and flashes of a white corridor, a frightened child resembling her younger self, Sera's sleeve, and a closing door. She has lied to a health monitor, rejected stabilization, and agreed with Ivo to seek a maintenance mirror that may reveal more without leaving a trace. She possesses her harbor implant, work clothes, tools, repair manual with copied code, blue seal, and archival unit; she is physically shaken, frightened, angry, and increasingly distrustful of official medical systems.

He has discovered that Mara is hiding a machine and knows she is not truly fine, though he does not understand HARBORLIGHT or the archival records. He fears she will be taken for stabilization and worries about who will repair the water if she disappears. He has agreed to conceal her condition from monitors and remains protective, observant, and anxious. He possesses his ordinary clothes and household belongings and is physically safe but emotionally frightened.

He knows the unit references HARBORLIGHT, emotional regulation, and altered public records, and has witnessed Mara's severe harbor reaction. He remains protective and argumentative, warning that Directorate systems may trace their investigation. He knows of a maintenance mirror beneath the old school terminal and has agreed to help Mara access it under strict limits: avoid traces, stop after a security ping, and attempt no heroics. chapters.name: The Song Under the Market
chapters.content:
The code did not lead to the old school.

It led around it.

Mara found the turn just before dawn, while the three of them sat beneath the workbench and listened to the archival unit tick itself awake. Ivo had spread the copied harbor syntax across the floor. Eli, forbidden to touch anything, was touching everything with his eyes.

“Here,” Mara said. “The routing mark repeats.”

Ivo leaned over her shoulder. “That’s not a route. It’s a maintenance designation.”

“Then why does it end in a song symbol?”

He frowned. The symbol looked like three hooked lines, a notation used in the oldest pump manuals for an acoustic calibration. Mara traced the neighboring marks with a grease-stained finger. “Lower market. Dock Nine. An oral key.”

“Or a corrupted file.”

“Everything is a corrupted file to you.”

“Everything is a trap to the Directorate.”

Eli raised his hand. “Are we going to the market?”

“No,” Mara and Ivo said together.

Eli lowered his hand. “That sounded like yes.”

By evening, it was yes.

The lower market clung to the eastern underside of New Carthage, a forest of patched platforms and canvas roofs strung beneath the official walkways. Water dripped from the city above in steady silver threads. The market smelled of brine, hot metal, yeast, and the sweet rot of kelp drying in baskets. Vendors shouted over one another: battery cells, boots made from sailcloth, counterfeit weather tabs, knives sharpened on bicycle rims.

Mara kept one hand on Eli’s shoulder. The other rested near the blue-sealed archival unit inside her coat. Since morning, her harbor had been sending her contradictory instructions.

CALM.

ALERT.

REPORT COGNITIVE IRREGULARITY.

She had silenced the display, but not the sensations. Her pulse felt too large for her body. Every sudden voice seemed to enter through her skin. The city’s lights shimmered at the edge of sight, leaving pale trails.

Ivo noticed. He noticed everything now.

“If you need to stop—”

“I’ll say.”

“You said that at the pump.”

“And I did not stop.”

“That is not the defense you think it is.”

They followed the maintenance mark through the market, past a woman selling bowls of red algae stew and a boy tossing copper washers into a tin cup. At the far end, beneath a collapsed crane, an old man sat on an overturned fuel drum. His back was bent almost double, but his hands were broad and knotted, the hands of someone who had hauled cable in storms.

He was singing.

The tune was familiar. Every child in New Carthage knew it. It was the founding song, taught in schools and played during Renewal ceremonies. Mara knew the official words by heart: Lift the harbor, light the way / We survived the drowning day.

But this man sang different words.

“When the sirens called the eastward fleet,
They sealed the gates beneath our feet.
The high ships turned where the flood ran white—
And left the Belt to drown that night.”

Mara stopped.

Eli’s fingers tightened around hers.

The old man continued, his voice thin but unwavering. Around him, people had begun to gather without appearing to gather. A woman selecting onions went still. Two dockhands leaned against a stack of crates. A child perched on a coil of rope, mouthing the lines.

Ivo whispered, “We should leave.”

The old man’s eyes opened. They were milky at the edges, sharp at the center.

“Blue seal,” he said. “You’re late, little machine girl.”

Mara’s mouth went dry. “Do you know me?”

“I know the seal. I know the question it brings.” He tapped the side of his head. “Names are harder. They keep trying to take those.”

“What’s your name?” Eli asked.

The old man smiled. “Dagan Pell. Dockworker, third shift, retired by the sea and not by the Directorate.”

He shifted on the drum. “Come closer. If you stand at the edge, you’ll hear only the lies people tell themselves about being brave.”

Mara brought Eli with her. Ivo stayed half a step behind, scanning the platforms.

Dagan sang another verse.

“Ships had room for all the poor,
But orders came from upper door.
Food was counted, names were crossed,
And every missing child was lost.”

The song moved through Mara like a current. Not a vision, not exactly. Yet her harbor fluttered, trying to classify the melody. Familiar cultural artifact. Unauthorized historical variation. Emotional hazard.

She saw, for one instant, a wall covered in wet names. A woman’s hand wrote quickly. Sera’s yellow sleeve brushed the edge of the image.

Mara jerked back.

Dagan stopped singing. “You saw it.”

“I saw nothing.”

“Good. That means the machine hasn’t taken everything.”

Ivo crouched beside her. “What do you mean, oral key?”

Dagan’s gaze moved to him. “You’ve got the mouth of a locked drawer.”

“People say that.”

“People are often right by accident.” Dagan pointed to the unit beneath Mara’s coat. “The old harbor systems used songs to verify what paper denied. Before the Directorate cleaned the records, dock crews carried the routes in their heads. Which ships went where. Which neighborhoods got sealed. Who was aboard. Who was ordered to wait.”

“Why songs?” Mara asked.

“Because inspectors can confiscate a book. They can’t confiscate every grandmother’s kitchen.”

A woman with flour on her sleeves spoke from the crowd. “My mother taught us to fold seaweed cakes in the shape of the evacuation map.”

“And my brothers played a game,” said one of the dockhands. “Red buoy meant the eastern district. If you stepped on it, you were dead.”

“Murals,” said another voice. “They painted the ships under bridges. Directorate crews scrubbed them, so people painted them again.”

Dagan nodded. “The city remembers in pieces. A song here. A recipe there. A child’s game. A blue line under a table. Official archives are tidy because they have been frightened into tidiness.”

Mara drew the archival unit from her coat. The blue seal caught the market light.

Dagan did not reach for it. “You found one.”

“It has code referencing HARBORLIGHT,” Mara said. “Emotional regulation. Altered records. Years after the rise.”

Several people made small sounds—not surprise, but recognition.

Dagan’s expression hardened. “Then you need the names before you need the machine.”

“Whose names?”

“The ones who refused the clean story.”

Before he could say more, a bell rang above the market.

Not a vendor’s bell. Three flat notes, followed by silence.

The crowd changed. Faces turned toward the entrances. Stalls folded with practiced speed. A woman snatched her onions into a sack. The child on the rope disappeared beneath it.

“Directorate,” Ivo said.

At the northern platform, white-coated officers stepped through the hanging tarps. Their armor was clean enough to look unreal in the market’s grease and rain. A drone floated above them, its lens turning.

“Public health inspection,” called the lead officer. “Remain where you are. Unlicensed assembly is a contagion-risk behavior.”

Dagan laughed once. “They’ve improved the song.”

Mara’s harbor pulsed.

COMPLY FOR SAFETY.

She grabbed Eli and pulled him behind the fuel drum. Ivo kicked a crate into the path of the first officer. It burst open, spilling copper washers like bright seeds.

The market erupted.

People ran in every direction, not blindly but along routes they had learned through years of raids. Canvas dropped. Steam valves opened. Someone threw a sack of powdered lime into the drone’s lens. The machine shrieked and fired a warning pulse that struck a metal roof, showering sparks.

“Tunnel!” Ivo shouted.

Dagan seized Mara’s wrist with startling strength. “Under the fish tables. Third hatch.”

“Come with us.”

“I’m slower than a story and twice as stubborn.” He pushed something into her palm: folded paper, warm from his coat. “Take this. Don’t open it in the light.”

An officer shouted, “Mara Venn!”

The name struck harder than the warning pulse. Her harbor flashed red. Eli cried out. Ivo shoved her toward the tables.

“Move!”

They dove beneath a stall as boots thundered overhead. The third hatch was hidden under a mat of woven kelp. Ivo pried it up with his wrench. A breath of cold, foul air rose from below.

Eli went first. Mara followed, then Ivo pulled the hatch shut above them.

The tunnel was barely wide enough for their shoulders. Black water covered the floor to Mara’s ankles. Pipes crossed the ceiling, sweating rust. Behind them came muffled orders and the crash of overturned stalls.

Eli was breathing too fast.

“Look at me,” Mara whispered. “Count the bolts.”

“There are too many.”

“Then count the ones you can see.”

“One. Two. Three—”

Ivo led them by the weak green glow of maintenance paint. At the first junction, a patrol light swept across the hatch behind them. Mara’s heart lurched. Her harbor offered three simultaneous instructions, each stamped urgent.

She pressed her palm to the wall and felt the city’s old vibration: pumps, valves, hidden currents. The contradictory signals in her implant tangled with the tunnel’s machinery. For a moment the patrol light flickered, uncertain.

Ivo looked back. “Did you do that?”

“I don’t know.”

“Excellent. Terrifying, but excellent.”

They ran until the market noise faded. The tunnel opened beneath an abandoned laundry room near the old school terminal. They climbed out soaked and shaking.

Only then did Mara unfold Dagan’s paper.

It was covered in names, written in several hands. Dockworkers. Teachers. Children. Whole families. Beside some names were dates; beside others, a ship number or a single word: refused, vanished, witnessed.

Near the bottom, in dark blue ink, was SERA VENN.

No date. No explanation. Just a small mark like three hooked lines.

Eli leaned close. “Is that Mum?”

Mara could not answer.

Ivo read over her shoulder. “Dagan said names before machines.”

At the top of the page, someone had written: Find the Rememberers beneath the place where children learned to tell the truth.

Mara looked toward the old school terminal, its windows blind with salt.

“Who are the Rememberers?” Eli asked.

She folded the list and tucked it inside her shirt, against the harbor that would not stop warning her.

“I think,” she said, “we’re going to find out.”

chapters.name: The Rememberers
chapters.content:
## Chapter 4: The Rememberers

The laundry room had no windows, only a square vent crusted with salt and a drain that coughed whenever the tide shifted beneath the old terminal. Mara sat on an overturned detergent crate with her back against a rusted washer, holding Dagan Pell’s list inside her shirt.

Water ticked from her hair to the floor.

Eli had stopped shivering, but only because Ivo had wrapped him in a torn boiler blanket and made him drink warm water from a maintenance flask. The boy sat cross-legged beside the dryer, watching the door as if officers might come through the metal itself.

“How long?” Mara asked.

Ivo was crouched at the lock, one eye pressed to a crack in the frame. “Long enough for the search teams to decide the tunnel collapsed. Not long enough for us to become part of the furniture.”

“Dagan said beneath the old school.”

“He also said the old school was watched.”

“He said the school was forgotten.”

“Those are not opposites.”

Ivo rose and rubbed water from his face. His cheek was scraped, and a dark line of market silt ran along his jaw. He looked older than sixteen in the weak blue light, which made Mara angry at the Directorate, at Dagan, at the list beneath her shirt, and finally at herself for having no one to blame who could be reached.

Eli tugged the blanket tighter. “Are the Rememberers real?”

“I hope not,” Ivo said.

Mara looked at him.

“I mean,” he continued, “I hope they are not the sort of people who collect frightened children and make speeches about sacrifice.”

“They preserve things,” Mara said.

“People who preserve things usually want something.”

“So do mechanics.”

“Mechanics want working pumps.”

“Not always.”

That silenced him. The archival unit rested in Mara’s tool bag, wrapped in the repair manual and two oily work shirts. Since the raid, it seemed to have acquired a weight beyond metal. It dragged at her shoulder whenever she moved, as if the machine wanted to pull her toward the place where its secrets had been buried.

Ivo opened the door a finger’s width. The corridor beyond was empty except for drifting steam.

“Come on,” he said. “Before the school remembers it has a roof.”

They left through a service passage that sloped upward beneath the terminal. The old school stood on a narrow platform between two inhabited pontoons, its classrooms sealed after the lower foundations flooded. The Directorate had built a new school in the upper ring, where the floors stayed dry and children learned that the sea rise had been a weather event, tragic but blameless. The old building had no power, no registered caretaker, and a warning placard declaring it structurally unstable.

Ivo pried the placard loose.

Behind it, set in the wall, was a maintenance hatch.

The hatch accepted his wire coil after three attempts. A green light blinked once, then died.

“Encouraging,” he murmured.

The passage beyond smelled of chalk, mold, and iron. Mara followed Ivo through darkness while Eli held the back of her coat. Their shoes struck the submerged floor with soft splashes. Faded painted letters appeared on the walls: A, B, C, then a row of numbers interrupted by a black tide mark.

At the end of the corridor stood a classroom door. Someone had painted a hooked line across it in white grease pencil.

Mara’s harbor warmed beneath her skin.

The warning came first: UNAUTHORIZED COGNITIVE STIMULUS.

Then the opposite: RECOGNITION RESPONSE—SAFE.

She caught the doorframe.

Ivo turned. “Mara?”

“I’m fine.”

“Your eyes are doing that thing.”

“What thing?”

“Looking at something that isn’t here.”

Eli’s fingers tightened on her coat. “Don’t say anything to the school.”

The door opened inward.

A woman stood on the other side holding a hand-cranked pistol-shaped device. She was perhaps sixty, with silver hair cut close to her skull and a green cardigan patched at both elbows. Her eyes moved from Ivo to Mara to Eli, then settled on the tool bag.

“Name,” she said.

“Ivo Renn.”

“I know yours.”

Her gaze sharpened on Mara. “Mara Venn.”

The room seemed to contract. Somewhere in the building, water struck a pipe in a slow, measured rhythm.

Ivo stepped in front of Eli. “We were sent by Dagan Pell.”

“Dagan sends everyone when he thinks the weather is turning.”

“He gave us this.”

Mara drew out the folded list. The woman did not take it. She studied the hooked line beside Sera’s name, then lowered the weapon.

“Anja Quill,” she said. “Come inside before your harbor announces you to the whole foundation.”

The classroom had been transformed. Desks were stacked against one wall, their surfaces covered with handwritten pages. Shelves filled the blackboard recesses. Books stood in rows, bound with thread, wire, cloth strips, and once, Mara noticed, a child’s red shoelace. A mechanical recorder occupied the teacher’s desk, its brass cylinder shining under a hooded lamp. Beside it sat three smaller machines with turning handles and wax drums.

Eli stared at the books.

“Are they real?” he asked.

Anja’s expression softened. “More real than most things printed by the Directorate.”

A man’s voice came from the back of the room. “That is a poor standard.”

He emerged between two shelves carrying a crate of metal plates. He was broad-shouldered and bearded, with a left hand missing two fingers. His coat bore the faded orange stripe of the dockworkers’ union, though the union itself had been absorbed into the Civic Allocation Office years ago.

“Tomas Vale,” he said. “Organizer, loader, occasional criminal.”

“Frequent criminal,” Anja said.

“Only where the law is badly written.”

His eyes found Mara’s tool bag. “Is that the unit?”

Mara did not answer.

Tomas set down the crate. “Then we have wasted enough time.”

Anja held out her hand. “We have not even established whether she is followed.”

“If she were followed, the officers would already be here.”

“Unless they want to see where she leads us.”

Tomas looked toward the walls, as if the old school might be listening. “We should move the archive.”

“Where?”

“Somewhere the Directorate cannot reach.”

“Such a place does not exist.”

“Then somewhere it costs them to reach.”

Their argument had the worn familiarity of people who had been having it for years. Mara felt a strange, unwelcome relief. The Rememberers were not a single hidden mind. They disagreed, interrupted, and failed to notice Eli creeping toward a shelf of small illustrated books.

Anja saw him and said, “Those are not toys.”

“I know.”

“Then you are ahead of some adults.”

Mara placed the archival unit on a desk. The room changed around it. Anja went still. Tomas swore under his breath.

The casing was blue beneath its grime, its municipal seal scored by a diagonal scratch. Mara removed the repair manual and laid out the copied code. She expected questions. Instead, Anja reached for the page as though it might burn her.

“Where did you get this?”

“Government records building under the east ruins.”

“Who else touched it?”

“Ivo. Me.”

“And the Directorate?”

“They tried.”

Tomas gave a humorless laugh. “Good.”

Anja ignored him. She rotated the unit and examined the ports, the old seal, the fracture Mara had soldered. “This was not an archive in the ordinary sense.”

“It played a recording,” Mara said. “A voice.”

“Whose?”

Mara’s throat tightened. “My mother’s.”

No one moved.

Anja looked at the list. “Sera Venn.”

“You know her?”

“I knew of her.”

“That is not an answer.”

“No,” Anja said. “It is the answer I can give before I know what you are prepared to hear.”

Tomas struck the desk with his palm. The recorder’s brass cylinder trembled. “We have spent twelve years preserving evidence while the city is fed lies. If Sera’s daughter has brought us a live HARBORLIGHT unit, we should use it.”

“Use it for what?” Mara asked.

“To open the system.”

“Can you?”

“Not yet.”

“Then what do you mean?”

“Find the relay. Break the compliance channels. Let every harbor in New Carthage hear what was taken from them.”

Eli had returned to Mara’s side. His face had gone pale. “Would that fix people?”

Tomas glanced down at him. “It would wake them.”

“Waking hurts,” Anja said.

Tomas’s jaw hardened. “So does sleeping in a burning room.”

Anja turned to Mara. “HARBORLIGHT began as a medical system. After the sea rise, the city’s population suffered mass trauma: panic seizures, grief disorders, violent episodes, memory fragmentation. The first engineers designed emotional regulation—limited, therapeutic, voluntary.”

“Voluntary,” Mara repeated.

“For a short time.” Anja touched the blue casing with one finger. “Then the Directorate discovered that a person whose fear could be reduced could also be made less likely to resist. A person whose grief could be softened would stop asking where the dead had gone. They integrated the system into harbor implants, schools, work assignments, food access, medical records.”

Mara’s skin crawled beneath the implant. “You said memory.”

“It was added later. At first, HARBORLIGHT altered the intensity of recall. Then the engineers learned to interrupt association, to remove names from one memory and replace them with approved explanations. Storm death. Relocation. Treatment failure. Administrative error.”

“Sera knew?”

“Some of the engineers knew. Sera discovered the full function.”

The room blurred. Mara gripped the desk. Her mother in a yellow sleeve. A wall of names. A hand reaching through rain.

Her harbor flashed conflicting notices across her vision.

STABILIZATION RECOMMENDED.

MEMORY VERIFIED.

MEMORY UNVERIFIED.

DO NOT TRUST—

She shut her eyes.

Anja’s voice came carefully. “What is it showing you?”

“Nothing I can prove.”

“That may be the most important answer.”

Tomas turned toward the recorder. “Proof does not feed people.”

“No,” Anja said. “But panic starves them faster. If we release damaged memories without medical support, people may collapse. If we sabotage the central system without separating its medical functions, thousands could suffer seizures, psychosis, or death.”

“Then we separate them.”

“With what technicians? Which maps? Which safeguards? You want an uprising because you are angry.”

“I am angry because they made obedience out of my dead brother.”

The words landed harder than his fist had. Tomas looked away.

Mara thought of Eli forgetting their mother’s face. She thought of Dagan singing names into a room full of people who had learned not to trust their own minds. She thought of her own harbor, issuing two truths at once and calling both health.

“What do the Rememberers want from me?” she asked.

Anja answered first. “The truth about the unit. What it contains, how it responds to you, and whether the recording can be recovered without damaging it.”

Tomas said, “A choice.”

“What choice?”

“Whether you want to help us end this.”

Mara looked at the shelves. Every handmade book seemed to lean toward her. Some held names. Some held recipes, songs, drawings, testimony from people who had survived the same official past in different bodies. None of them looked like a weapon. Together, they looked heavier than one.

“I don’t trust you,” she said.

“Good,” Anja replied. “Trust should be earned.”

Tomas gave a short nod. “Distrust the Directorate more.”

“I already do.”

Anja pulled a chair beneath the lamp. “Then sit. We will make a copy of your code, examine the unit, and compare your mother’s recording with what we have preserved. No one touches your harbor. No one touches the boy. And no broadcast, sabotage, or heroic gesture happens in this room without everyone understanding the cost.”

Tomas opened his mouth.

“Everyone,” Anja repeated.

He closed it.

Mara sat. Eli leaned against her shoulder, still wrapped in the boiler blanket. Ivo took up a position near the door, watching the corridor and the strangers alike.

Anja began turning the recorder’s crank. The cylinder whispered, then clicked into motion.

For the first time since the market raid, Mara heard something other than pursuit: the soft mechanical sound of people refusing to let the past disappear.
