“Write the proposal,” she said. “Write who opposed it. Write what evidence they offered. If the vote changes after new information, preserve the first vote too.”

A young clerk raised her hand. “Won’t that make us look divided?”

“We are divided,” Anja said. “The question is whether the division is visible enough to be negotiated.”

Mara looked toward the children’s room. Eli was there with Nia and six others, painting a lesson wall in broad blue strokes. He had drawn a flooded stairwell, then added three doors, each labeled in his careful lettering: *I SAW THIS*, *I THINK THIS*, and *SOMEONE TOLD ME*. Nia was painting a red square beneath the third door. When Mara caught her eye, the girl lifted the faded strip of cloth tied around her wrist and gave a small, solemn wave.

The movement had learned to build rooms before it learned to win arguments. Free schools occupied empty ferry sheds and storage decks. Repair yards accepted broken pumps whether or not the owner could pay. Councils met beside kitchens, clinics, and laundry lines. A memory house without food became a museum; a clinic without witnesses became another place where people were told what they had felt. So the work had to remain tangled.

Their first victory came over grain.

The Directorate still controlled the central reserve towers, but the lower districts had begun keeping public inventories. Every sack was marked when it entered a storehouse, when it was opened, and how many bowls it filled. Ivo’s couriers carried copies of the lists in waterproof sleeves. When the Directorate announced that shortages required emergency ration reductions, three neighborhoods produced records showing that the reserve towers held six weeks of grain.

The figures were argued over in public broadcasts for nine days. On the tenth, a Directorate barge arrived at the depot and unloaded forty crates.

Forty crates did not repair the theft of forty years. Mara knew this. She also knew the children ate that night.

The second victory was power. Tomas organized dock crews to refuse maintenance on the upper district’s decorative floodlights until the lower clinics received replacement cells. The Directorate called it sabotage. Tomas called it a work stoppage. Anja insisted that the distinction be recorded in both terms, along with the conditions that had produced it.

After eleven hours, the cells arrived.

That evening, Tomas found Mara on the depot roof, where she was checking a route ledger against three different witness copies. The floating city trembled beneath them. Distant turbines turned the black water into broken silver.

“You’ve made a religion of delay,” he said.

Mara kept her eyes on the ledger. “Delay is what we call preparation when you dislike the people doing it.”

“I dislike watching children study while the tower still stands.”

“The tower contains desalination controls, emergency relays, medical switching, and half the city’s weather anchors.”

“Then seize it.”

“With whom? The dockworkers? The clinic volunteers? The children carrying paintbrushes?”

“With everyone who is tired of asking permission.”

Mara closed the ledger. “People are tired of burying friends, too. That doesn’t mean they want us choosing which systems fail.”

Tomas leaned on the railing. His beard had gone gray at the chin since the prison break. “You speak as if administration is innocent.”

“It isn’t.”

“Every compromise gives them another month.”

“Every attack gives them a funeral and a speech.”

For a moment the only sound was the clank of the repair yard below. Then Tomas said, more quietly, “You are becoming very good at sounding like the people we fought.”

The words found the place in Mara that was already raw. She had slept four hours in two days. Her harbor had sent a low-priority fatigue notice, then contradicted itself with an alert for dangerous emotional flattening. She had laughed when she saw it, and then cried because the laugh had hurt.

“I am not a tower,” she said.

“No,” Tomas replied. “That is what I am trying to remind you.”

He left her with the ledger and the accusation.

Later, Ivo found her in the schoolroom, asleep sitting up beside a box of slate tablets. He did not wake her immediately. When she opened her eyes, he was crouched in front of her, holding out half a pear.

“You missed supper,” he said.

“I attended supper in spirit.”

“Your spirit has poor nutrition.”

She took the pear. His courier coat was patched at both shoulders, and the scar along his cheek had faded to a pale line. He had a new coil of wire looped through his belt, repaired with blue thread.

“How many routes?” she asked.

“Twenty-three active. Four suspected. Two I burned because an inspector started asking the right questions.”

“Did you eat?”

“Your spirit is contagious.”

She smiled, and the smile became too much. For a second she saw the old correction-facility corridor over the schoolroom wall: white panels, a red cup, Eli turning away. Her harbor chimed three different warnings. Ivo waited until the room settled.

“Information,” he said. “Not an order.”

Mara pressed her palms to her eyes. “I know.”

“You don’t have to know alone.”

“I am not alone.”

“I meant you don’t have to be the person who can carry everything.”

She lowered her hands. Children slept behind the partition, wrapped in donated blankets. Someone snored softly. The ordinary sound made the room feel more dangerous than a raid.

“People keep looking at me,” she said. “They ask what Mara thinks. What Mara will approve. They bring me their arguments as if I have a hidden drawer labeled *correct answer*.”

“You could tell them the drawer is empty.”

“I do.”

“They may need to hear it more than once.”

“I am tired of being useful.”

Ivo’s expression changed—not pity, which she could not bear, but recognition. “Then be useless with me for five minutes.”

He sat beside her on the floor. They listened to the rain ticking against the roof. His shoulder touched hers. The contact was small, almost accidental, and Mara felt her body register it before her harbor could classify it.

“Ivo,” she said.

“I know.”

“You don’t know what I was going to say.”

“I know that too.”

She laughed, quietly this time. He turned toward her. There were still maps to copy, reserve figures to verify, and a council at dawn about the school’s missing heating cells. There would always be another emergency waiting behind the one they had survived.

“I don’t know how to make a life,” Mara said.

“Neither do I.”

“I know how to make a route list.”

“I know how to lose one.”

“I know how to argue with Tomas.”

“That is a specialized civic skill.”

She looked at him. “If we do this properly, there may not be a private future.”

“There may not be a private present.”

“That isn’t reassuring.”

“No. But it’s honest.”

He took her hand. His fingers were rough from wire, rope, and engine housings. Mara let him hold it. She did not turn the moment into a promise. Promises had too often been used as locks. But when he kissed her, she felt no command in it, no signal from a machine, only a choice made and remade by two tired people.

In the morning, the heating cells did not arrive.

The school council met before sunrise. One proposal said to divert cells from the clinic dormitory. Another said to close classes for a week. A third, written by Eli in crooked blue letters, said: *Ask the repair yard to make something else.*

Mara almost dismissed it. Then she saw the children studying the page, waiting to learn whether their idea counted.

They opened the yard.

By midday, mechanics, teachers, and older students were taking apart dead lanterns, salvaged battery shells, and a failed desalination regulator. The work was slow and ugly. Two cells sparked. One exploded with a pop that sent everyone ducking. Nia began to cry, and Mara stopped the project until the medics checked every child.

No one called the pause defeat.

By evening, they had assembled six warming panels. They were inefficient, patched, and safe enough. The clinic kept its cells. The school stayed open.

Mara wrote the result into the public ledger: *Six panels produced. Labor: thirty-one people. Materials: disputed. Risks: recorded. Method: repeatable, perhaps.*

Anja read over her shoulder. “Perhaps?”

“Perhaps is accurate.”

“It is also a beginning.”

Below them, the children crowded around the new panels. Eli had painted a small sun on each one, not because the panels made sunlight, but because he said warmth deserved a picture.

Mara watched Tomas distribute tools, Ivo carry a crate, and Anja correct a clerk who had omitted a dissenting vote. No one was waiting for a hero to descend from the tower. They were learning where the bolts went, who had the spare parts, which promises needed witnesses, and how to stop when stopping kept someone alive.

Courage had brought them through the locked doors. Trust, Mara understood, would have to be built one hinge at a time.

set.name: Mara Venn
set.description: Mara is based temporarily at the old ferry depot, which functions as a free school, communal repair yard, food store, and neighborhood council hall, while continuing to coordinate the decentralized network across floating districts. She organizes public inventories, schools, repair work, and witnessed decisions; she knows the movement has forced limited Directorate concessions in grain and energy, but remains alert to retaliation and propaganda. Tomas presses her toward direct attacks, while Anja supports process but warns against compromise becoming obedience. Mara and Ivo have acknowledged mutual love and begun a relationship, though neither sees an easy private future. Mara is exhausted and physically strained by her contradictory harbor, which produces conflicting alerts that she treats as information rather than commands. She is increasingly troubled by people treating her as a symbol or final authority. She carries route ledgers, public decision records, and notebooks, and is learning that trust requires patient, transparent administration as well as courage.

set.name: Eli Venn
set.description: Eli is at the old ferry depot school with Nia and other children, turning uncertain memory fragments into murals and visual lessons. He has painted categories distinguishing direct sight, belief, and hearsay, and proposed involving children in the safe repair of heating panels. He recognizes Mara through voice, phrases, and habits while remaining uncertain about her face and other family memories. He carries paints and drawing supplies, is emotionally recovering, and is becoming a participant in civic education rather than only a rescued child.

set.name: Ivo Renn
set.description: Ivo is based on the courier routes linking the floating districts, schools, clinics, repair yards, and memory houses, and is currently working from the old ferry depot. He has twenty-three active routes, has burned several suspected routes after surveillance, and carries a repaired wire coil, waterproof lists, and his patched courier coat. He helps transport food, energy information, tools, and archive copies while keeping the network decentralized. His friendship with Mara has deepened into mutual love, though both recognize that their work leaves little room for a private future. He remains physically marked by a persistent limp and healing scar, and watches Mara for exhaustion and harbor overload while respecting her autonomy.

set.name: Anja Quill
set.description: Anja is working at the old ferry depot and traveling among council training rooms, memory houses, clinics, and schools. She trains clerks and archivists to preserve proposals, dissent, evidence, changing votes, consent, and uncertainty rather than presenting decisions as unquestionable truth. She supports Mara's decentralized civic strategy but warns that compromise can become obedience. She is intellectually precise and physically tired, and continues safeguarding technical and historical knowledge while helping ensure practical care accompanies memory work.

set.name: Tomas Vale
set.description: Tomas is working with dock crews, district councils, and communal repair yards from the old ferry depot. He helped organize a work stoppage that forced the Directorate to provide energy cells to lower-district clinics and schools, but remains impatient with negotiation and favors direct action against the central tower. He respects practical infrastructure and dockworker authority while challenging Mara's refusal to authorize attacks. He is physically weathered, with a graying beard, and emotionally frustrated by the movement's slow pace.

set.name: Nia
set.description: Nia is living and learning at the old ferry depot school with other rescued children. She participates in visual-history lessons, paints uncertain images, and still wears the faded red family cloth around her wrist. She remains frightened by sudden sounds and uncertain about her family memories but is receiving protection, schooling, and care without forced replacement stories.

Across the floating districts, Mara helped establish free schools, communal repair yards, and neighborhood councils that combined education, practical maintenance, food distribution, and witnessed decision-making.

Public inventories and coordinated dockworker work stoppages forced the Directorate to release food reserves and energy cells to lower-district communities without destroying essential infrastructure.
Mara and Ivo acknowledged their love and began a relationship while accepting that their organizing work left little room for a private future.

Mara learned through a failed heating-cell project that patient administration, transparent dissent, safety pauses, and repeatable repair were as necessary to changing the city as courage and protest.

chapters.name: The Counterhistory
chapters.content:
## The Counterhistory

The first Directorate broadcast arrived during breakfast, between the inventory of grain and the weather report.

The depot’s receiver clicked, hissed, and filled the schoolroom with Minister Cassian Or’s measured voice.

“New Carthage has never denied that mistakes were made during the first years after the sea rise,” he said. “Records now released by the Stability Ministry confirm that certain officials concealed ration losses, misclassified detainees, and authorized unnecessary harbor interventions. These abuses were real. They were investigated. They were corrected.”

Mara stopped spreading paste on a piece of bread.

Around the long tables, people turned toward the speaker. A child dropped a spoon. In the repair yard beyond the open doors, a hammer struck metal and then went silent.

Cassian continued. “But the existence of misconduct does not invalidate the structure that saved this city. The founding families prevented a greater disaster: civil war among the evacuation fleets, mass panic during the flooding, and the collapse of the medical harbor lattice. Stability was not tyranny. It was triage.”

The broadcast named no families. It displayed their seals instead, elegant circles and hooked stars that every citizen recognized from towers, schools, and food crates.

Then Mara’s name appeared in a subtitle beneath the voice.

**MARA VENN: ORGANIZER, HARBOR MANIPULATOR, EXPLOITER OF CHILD TRAUMA.**

The room seemed to narrow around her.

“Those who now parade distressed children before cameras,” Cassian said, “must answer whether grief is being used as a political weapon. A memory is not a verdict. A frightened drawing is not a legal record. We invite all citizens to reject theatrical history and return to accountable institutions.”

Eli stood at the far end of the room, paint on his wrist. He stared at the receiver as if it had spoken in his own voice.

Mara crossed the room and switched it off.

For several breaths nobody moved.

“Is a drawing a weapon?” Nia asked.

“Not by itself,” Eli said. He looked at Mara. “Can someone make it one?”

“Yes,” Mara answered. “Anyone can use anything to hurt someone. A drawing. A law. A true story. That is why we show how it was made and let people question it.”

A courier arrived before noon with a second message: Cassian had released the edited archives to every public terminal. The files included ration ledgers, detention summaries, medical directives, and a three-hundred-page history titled *The Necessary Harbor*. The Directorate admitted enough wrongdoing to appear fearless. It included photographs of obsolete officials being stripped of rank, as if a few punished clerks could absorb the weight of a system.

The archive’s omissions were more revealing than its admissions. There were no emergency votes. No protest index. No names from the diverted evacuation ships. No mention of the correction facility’s children except as “neurologically vulnerable dependents rescued through state intervention.”

At the afternoon council, Tomas slammed a printed page onto the table.

“They admit the detentions,” he said. “They call them regrettable. We call them what they were.”

“Both words can be recorded,” Anja said.

“Not when one is designed to soften the other.”

Mara read the page. It described the Salvage Belt raid as a temporary health operation conducted after “credible evidence of contagious cognitive agitation.” Her own name appeared six times. Eli’s appeared once, as a dependent whose “distress was amplified by irresponsible adult messaging.”

“They are making the children evidence against us,” Mara said.

“They are making us evidence against ourselves,” Anja replied. “If we answer with a simpler story, they will win the argument about complexity.”

Tomas’s hand tightened on the table. “People do not eat complexity.”

“No,” Mara said. “They eat bread. Complexity is what tells us where the bread went.”

The first public debate took place three days later in an upper-district assembly hall. For years the hall had hosted ceremonies in which citizens repeated approved gratitude beneath blue glass. Now the doors stood open, and lower-district residents arrived in patched coats while upper-district families entered with security escorts who pretended not to be guards.

Mara sat beneath no platform and refused the offered lectern. Ivo had arranged three routes out of the building, though he claimed they were merely practical precautions. His limp was worse in cold weather; he leaned against a brass rail and watched every doorway.

A woman in a white wool coat rose first.

“My grandparents kept the western fleet together,” she said. “They had minutes to decide. If they had opened every archive and convened every frightened passenger, no one would have survived. You speak of consent as though storms ask permission.”

A dockworker answered from the rear. “The storm did not sign the orders.”

“Neither did my grandmother,” the woman said. “She inherited a catastrophe.”

Mara felt the room tilt toward two clean stories: villains who had chosen every death, or guardians who had been forced into every cruelty. Both were easier than the truth, which contained cowardice, calculation, terror, and people making choices inside systems they had helped build.

“Your grandmother may have inherited a catastrophe,” Mara said, standing. “The question is what she did with the power that followed. We have records showing evacuation fuel was diverted to industrial platforms. We have testimony from families left behind. We also have gaps. Where the record is incomplete, we must say so.”

A man near the front called, “You admit the archive is unreliable?”

“I admit every archive requires examination.”

“Even yours?”

“Especially ours.”

That answer traveled faster than any speech. By evening, upper-district residents were copying the movement’s meeting schedules. Some came to the memory houses carrying family documents. Others arrived demanding stronger patrols, claiming the debates proved that the lower districts were preparing revenge.

Then Pell found the error.

She came to Mara after dusk with her mechanical recorder tucked under one arm and a consent ledger under the other. Her face was pale.

“The testimony from North Quay,” she said. “The one about the children locked in the grain office.”

“What about it?”

“The recorder’s second head captured the interview before Tomas edited the public copy. The witness saw six children. The distributed transcript says nineteen.”

Mara looked at the ledger. “Why was it changed?”

Pell swallowed. “A volunteer thought six would sound too small. She said the larger number represented the whole pattern.”

“Did the witness approve that?”

“No.”

The room behind them held shelves of copied statements, each wrapped in waxed cloth. Mara imagined Cassian opening this discovery like a gift.

“Any other changes?” she asked.

Pell hesitated. “The South Reservoir account says soldiers fired into a crowd. The witness heard shots and saw people fall, but did not see who fired. The transcript names Directorate soldiers.”

“Who added that?”

“Three people argued that everyone knew it was them.”

Everyone knew. The phrase had built more cages than steel.

Mara spent the night comparing originals, copies, and public summaries. By dawn, she had identified seven altered details: an inflated number of detainees, a date moved by two days, a statement converted from “I think” to “I saw,” a uniform described from memory as a Directorate insignia, and three deaths assigned causes no witness had verified.

The errors did not erase the pattern. The correction facility had existed. Children had been conditioned. The Directorate had raided the Belt. But the errors gave Cassian a weapon and gave frightened citizens reason to distrust every grieving voice.

Tomas entered while Mara was writing the corrections.

“You’re pulling the teeth from our evidence,” he said.

“I’m removing teeth that were never there.”

“Cassian will broadcast this as proof that we lied.”

“We did lie.”

The word struck harder than she intended. Tomas stared at her.

“Some of us did,” she continued. “Some exaggerated. Some guessed. Some thought a true pattern permitted false details. It does not.”

“You would hand him the knife.”

“I would stop holding it for him.”

Anja stood in the doorway. She looked older than she had the week before, though Mara knew that was impossible. “The question is not whether the movement can appear pure,” she said. “It is whether people can tell the difference between our mistake and the Directorate’s method.”

“What difference?” Tomas asked.

“We correct ourselves in public. They correct the record in secret and call the correction truth.”

Mara carried the original recordings to the evening assembly. The hall was fuller than before. Someone had painted a black stripe over her subtitle on the public terminal, but the words showed through.

She did not begin with the Directorate’s crimes. She began with the movement’s failures.

“We changed seven details in records that belong to other people,” she said. “We enlarged numbers, supplied certainty, and presented conclusions as observation. That was wrong. It harmed the witnesses and weakened everyone who needs to know what happened.”

A murmur moved through the hall. Someone shouted, “Traitor.” Someone else shouted, “At last.”

Mara held up Pell’s recorder.

“Here are the original sounds. Here are the witnesses’ permissions, and where permission was not given, the public copies will be withdrawn. The corrected files will show what is known, what is believed, and what remains unverified. The Directorate may use our honesty against us. It may already be doing so. We will not answer manipulation with a better-shaped manipulation.”

A young man in a security-blue jacket rose. “Then why should anyone believe you?”

“You shouldn’t believe me because I ask.”

The room quieted.

“Check the records. Ask the witnesses. Compare our copies with copies held in other districts. If we refuse questions, leave the meeting. If we hide a correction, expose us. If the Directorate refuses the same standard, record that too.”

For a moment she expected the words to collapse the movement. There would be no clean outrage now, no single account that could pass from mouth to mouth without resistance. Tomas did not look at her. Several young activists left through the side doors.

But the woman in the white coat remained seated. After the meeting, she approached Anja with a box of family papers. A teacher from the upper district asked Pell how to record uncertainty. The security-blue young man returned the next morning with a list of names from his own family’s ration office and said, awkwardly, “I don’t know what these prove.”

“Good,” Mara told him. “Start there.”

At the depot, Eli had added a fourth door to his mural. Beneath it he had written: *I WAS WRONG ABOUT THIS.*

Mara stood before it until he came beside her.

“Is that door bad?” he asked.

“No.”

“It feels bad.”

“Being wrong can hurt. Hiding it makes the hurt spread.”

He considered this, then dipped his brush in yellow. “I’m going to paint a handle.”

Outside, Cassian’s broadcast began again, polished and patient, promising that only the Directorate could protect citizens from dangerous uncertainty. Inside, Anja taught clerks to preserve dissent. Pell made duplicate recordings. Ivo marked new routes on a waterproof map. Tomas led a meeting of dockworkers who were angry with Mara and still intended to repair the west pumps.

The movement did not become stronger because everyone agreed. It became harder to counterfeit because disagreement remained visible.

Mara listened to the receiver until Cassian’s voice blurred beneath the hammering from the yard. Then she opened the public ledger and wrote the day’s first entry:

*Our account contains errors. The errors are named. The work continues.*

chapters.name: The Blackout Riot
chapters.content:
## The Blackout Riot

The first failure was not darkness.

It was the sound of every pump stopping at once.

Mara heard it through the old ferry depot walls: a long descending shudder, metal losing its argument with pressure. The repair yard went quiet. The school lamps blinked, recovered, and then vanished. In the food store, the refrigeration coils gave a final cough. Somewhere below the building, a valve slammed shut hard enough to tremble the floorboards.

For three breaths nobody moved.

Then the children began to cry.

“Lanterns,” Mara said. Her voice came out too calm, and the harbor behind her eyes marked the calm as suspicious. “Not all at once. Keep the blue cells for the clinic.”

Nia was already reaching for the emergency crate. Eli stood beside the mural wall, his paintbrush held upright in one hand. In the darkness, the faces he had painted seemed to multiply: flooded buildings, circles joined to circles, a red cup tipping forever toward an unseen edge.

“Is it the tower?” he asked.

“I don’t know.”

The harbor supplied three answers. LOCAL GRID FAULT. AUTHORIZED STABILITY MEASURE. HOSTILE INFRASTRUCTURE EVENT.

Mara closed her eyes until the letters dissolved.

A lantern flared. Anja appeared in its blue light with a paper inventory clutched against her chest. “The lower channels are down,” she said. “South Belt, Lantern Quays, and the raft moorings. Water pressure is falling in all three.”

Tomas came through the doorway behind her, soaked to the waist from the rain and furious enough to make the room feel smaller. “The upper districts still have power.”

“Confirmed?” Mara asked.

“People are calling from Crown Spire. Their windows are lit.” He struck the doorframe with his palm. “The Directorate has done this deliberately.”

“Then we need to move the reserves before the pipes drain.”

“Move them where? We have enough clean water for one day, perhaps two if the children drink half-rations.”

“Two days is not nothing.”

“It is nothing to a district that has already begun breaking into the public tanks.”

Ivo entered carrying a hand-cranked radio and a sack of signal mirrors. His patched coat was dark with rain, and the limp in his left leg was worse than usual. “Twenty-three routes,” he said. “Eight have stopped answering. The lower ferry locks are closed from the Directorate side.”

“Can the couriers get through?” Mara asked.

“Some. Not safely.”

A burst of static rose from the radio. Then a woman’s voice, clipped and official, filled the room.

“By order of the Ministry of Stability, temporary power restrictions have been enacted in response to coordinated infrastructure terrorism. Citizens are instructed to remain indoors, conserve water, and report unauthorized assemblies. Any harbor exhibiting irregular emotional output will be placed into permanent compliance mode for public protection.”

The message repeated.

Mara felt the words enter the room like a second darkness. Permanent compliance mode. The harbor would keep medical functions, Cassian had always claimed. It would remove panic, anger, disobedience—the distinctions his ministry called dangerous. It would make a person easier to keep alive and harder to recognize.

“Turn it off,” Tomas said.

Ivo lowered the volume, but the radio continued whispering under the rain.

“Cassian knew exactly when to do this,” Anja said. “He waited until the debate after your corrections had opened cracks.”

“Those cracks were there before me,” Mara said.

Tomas laughed without humor. “You corrected our own evidence in public, and now he has taken the corrections as proof that we are liars.”

Mara looked at him. “Some of us were wrong.”

“Some of us were trying to make people listen.”

“People deserve what is true, not what makes them useful.”

“And the people without water?” Tomas stepped closer. “Do they deserve your careful uncertainty?”

Before Mara could answer, a runner from Lantern Quays stumbled into the depot. He was perhaps fourteen, wearing a yellow scarf tied around his arm. Mud covered his knees.

“They’re at the eastern tanks,” he gasped. “The valves won’t open. Families are cutting the pipes.”

Anja caught him by the shoulders. “Are the clinic cells working?”

“For now.”

“For now,” Tomas repeated. “That is your practical preparation.”

Mara took the runner’s hand and felt the tremor there. “Ivo, send two repair crews to the tanks. No one goes alone. Anja, open the school kitchen and begin counting every container. Eli—”

“I’ll help,” Eli said.

“You will stay with Nia.”

“I can carry water.”

“You can help count it.”

His mouth tightened, but he nodded. The harbor gave no warning, only a soft, intermittent pulse behind her left ear. She had learned to fear that more than pain. Pain had boundaries. The pulse meant some buried system was trying to decide for her.

By midnight, the depot had become a map of shortages. Chalk marks appeared beside barrels and vanished when barrels emptied. The school kitchen boiled rainwater collected from tarps. Couriers arrived with reports from the dark districts: children fainting in stairwells, old people trapped in upper rooms because lifts had ceased, a clinic storing vaccines in wet cloth because its cooling unit had failed.

The Directorate had not attacked one system. It had attacked the distance between systems.

At the eastern tanks, a crowd had pulled down the chain fence. Tomas wanted the dock crews to take the main intake controls before morning. Mara found him in the rain, standing on a stack of shipping crates while young mechanics gathered below.

“Listen to me,” she said.

“No,” said a girl with grease-blackened cheeks. “We have listened for two years.”

Another voice rose behind her. “They shut our water off. Shut theirs off.”

The crowd answered with a hard, hungry roar.

Tomas raised both hands. “The central controls are beneath Crown Spire. If we seize them, the Directorate cannot starve the Belt again.”

“If we damage them,” Mara said, “the desalination lattice may fail across the city.”

“Then we take the controls intact.”

“With what technicians? With whose access codes? Half the people who know the system are in detention, and the other half are afraid.”

A boy called, “We can learn.”

“Not while the reservoirs are empty.”

The girl with the grease-blackened cheeks turned on Mara. “You told us truth was a kind of action.”

“It is. But it is not a pump.”

“Then what good is it?”

The question struck harder than the shouting. Mara looked past the crowd toward the black shape of the upper districts. Crown Spire rose above the rain like an illuminated bone. Its windows glowed steadily. Somewhere inside, people were washing dishes, charging harbors, sleeping under warm blankets, and hearing a broadcast that named Mara as the reason their city was afraid.

She had records. She had testimony. She had instructions for a future no one could yet reach.

She did not have water for the child crouched beside the fence, licking rain from his palm.

Ivo came up beside her. “We can send a delegation to the upper councils. The residents who attended the debates may not know what their ministers are doing. If they open their reservoirs—”

“They will not open them because we ask politely,” Tomas said.

“Some might if they hear the whole situation.”

“Some might,” Mara said. “Some will call the guards.”

“And some will help,” Ivo replied. “We have to reach those people before Tomas gives Cassian his war.”

Tomas climbed down from the crates. His face had gone still, which was more frightening than his anger. “Cassian already has his war. We are the only ones pretending it is a debate.”

The argument broke into three currents around them.

The negotiators wanted access to the upper reservoirs and a monitored restoration of the grid. They carried lists of names, proposed exchange terms, and written guarantees that no council would seize private stores without witness. The saboteurs wanted to cut the tower's relay cables and disable the compliance synchronization before it could begin. The tower group—mostly young mechanics, couriers, and children who had grown up under Directorate alarms—wanted to climb Crown Spire, occupy the control rooms, and broadcast from the top.

None of them trusted the others enough to share tools.

At dawn, the upper district confrontation began over a water convoy.

The Directorate sent six armored barges down the western channel, each carrying sealed tanks under guard. The convoy's public notice said the water was emergency relief for hospitals. A courier reported that three barges turned toward Crown Spire instead, while the lower districts' clinics received none.

Families from Lantern Quays blocked the channel with fishing skiffs. Upper-district residents came to the seawall, some carrying signs demanding open reservoirs, others carrying the Directorate's white stability flags. Mara reached the quay as the two crowds pressed against the security barricades.

“Back!” a Guardian shouted. “This is an unauthorized gathering.”

A bottle struck the barricade. Then another. Someone pulled the white flag from an old man's hands. A woman screamed that her brother was dying in a dark clinic. The Guardians raised shock rods.

Mara climbed onto a mooring post. “No one throw anything!”

Her voice vanished beneath the crowd.

A charge cracked across the seawall. The front line folded. People fell against one another, and panic became a physical tide. Someone fired from the upper promenade. No one could later agree whether the shot came from a Guardian weapon, an activist's stolen pistol, or a frightened citizen who had brought both rage and a gun to the same place.

The barricade broke.

Hundreds surged into the upper district. Windows shattered. A tram caught fire. Guardians fired into the smoke. Mara saw a child in a red coat disappear beneath running feet and tried to reach him, but Ivo caught her around the waist as the crowd drove them sideways.

“Not there!” he shouted. “Mara, not there!”

“I saw—”

“I know.”

The harbor screamed contradictory instructions. MOVE. FREEZE. TRIAGE. OBEY. Her vision flashed white, then filled with the drowned street from years ago. Sera stood beneath a torn banner, one hand raised, calling through water and sirens.

Not a command, Mara remembered.

A warning.

By evening the official number of dead was eighty-four. The clinic ledgers counted two hundred and nineteen. By the following morning, when the eastern hospitals began sending their lists through Ivo's routes, the number had passed four hundred. The exact count remained uncertain because the Directorate had shut down the civic registry along with the water system.

Cassian's broadcast came at sunset.

“Today, terrorist agitators transformed a lawful emergency into mass murder. Mara Venn and her extremist network are responsible for the deaths of our citizens. To prevent further contagion, every harbor in New Carthage will soon be placed into permanent compliance mode. This measure will preserve medical stability and end the emotional violence exploited by the Rememberers.”

In the depot, no one spoke until the broadcast ended.

Then Tomas put both hands on the council table. “We take the tower tonight.”

Several young activists struck the table in agreement.

Anja looked at Mara. “If compliance begins during the assault, the harbor lattice could interpret the movement as a hostile seizure. It may lock medical access everywhere.”

“Then we destroy the controls before he can activate them,” Tomas said.

Mara stared at the inventory sheets spread between them. Six districts without reliable water. Four clinics on failing cells. Three food depots with less than forty-eight hours of stock. The courier routes splitting under fear. The public archive full of truths that could not be eaten, and a movement that had mistaken being morally right for being ready.

She picked up a piece of chalk and drew three columns on the table: NEGOTIATE. SABOTAGE. SEIZE.

Under each heading she wrote the same question.

IF THIS WORKS, WHO KEEPS PEOPLE ALIVE TOMORROW?

Tomas pushed the chalk away. “You are still making lists.”

“Yes,” Mara said. “Because people are dying where our lists should have been.”

The admission quieted even the activists.

She looked at Ivo, then Anja, then Tomas. “We will not attack the desalination controls tonight. We will not pretend negotiation is enough either. At first light, every route becomes an emergency supply route. We ask upper-district residents to open reservoirs publicly, with witnesses. We send technicians to the tower—not to surrender, and not to burn it, but to identify the synchronization access points. If the Directorate moves to permanent compliance, we need a way to separate the medical lattice before we stop anything.”

“And if they refuse?” Tomas asked.

“Then we decide with food, water, medical teams, and people at every district assembly. Not with hunger behind us and fire in front.”

Tomas's expression hardened. “That is not a decision. That is delay.”

“No,” Mara said. “It is preparation.”

Outside, somewhere beyond the dark windows, a crowd began chanting for the tower.

A different crowd answered with a chant for open water.

Between them, the depot's last pump shuddered back to life, pushing a narrow stream through the pipes. Children cheered. Adults ran for containers. Mara listened to the water strike metal and understood, with a clarity more painful than any harbor alert, that truth could free a people only if someone had built them a place to stand when the ground moved.

She took up the route ledger.

The pages were not enough.

They would have to become enough.
