chapters.name: When the Harbors Open
chapters.content:
## Chapter 23: When the Harbors Open

For the first hour after the broadcast, New Carthage forgot how to be a city.

At the central relay, the air filled with overlapping voices. People called through open channels to ask whether a name they had heard belonged to a mother, a grandfather, a neighbor who had supposedly drowned. Others demanded that the transmission stop. Some districts paused the archive; some resumed it after ten minutes; some had no working pause signal and sent runners instead, carrying red cloths to clinics and blue lamps to assembly rooms.

The relay's floor trembled beneath Mara's boots. Every few seconds, an alarm blinked and went dark.

“South Belt reports a seizure cluster,” Anja said. She stood over three consoles, her medical case open at her feet. “Not all are harbor-related. Mark the distinction. Do not call every frightened person unstable.”

Pell turned a recorder's crank. “Lantern Quays has stopped the historical sequence. They are continuing the care instructions.”

“Good,” Mara said, though the word came out thin. Her hand was still locked around Ivo's. “Tell them to keep the pause public. No shame, no pressure to resume.”

A new voice burst from the speaker. “Upper Reservoir Twelve is being opened by residents. They say the private gates are not private anymore.”

Tomas gave a harsh laugh. “At last, the rich discover valves.”

“Record who opened them,” Anja said. “And how much. Anger is not a water ledger.”

Mara looked toward Cassian. He had not moved from the relay column. The broadcast had left his face gray, but the harbor lights still pulsed along his collar, reporting signals he no longer seemed able to command. His daughter's name had appeared in one of the casualty lists. Then a testimony from a woman who had held the child's hand at a flooded checkpoint. Cassian had listened without asking whether the memory was officially verified.

Now a red indicator flashed beside him.

“Minister,” Pell said, “the Directorate command band is requesting authentication.”

Cassian lifted his wrist. The band recognized him, chimed, and displayed three words: MAINTAIN SOCIAL CALM.

He stared at them.

“Answer,” Tomas said. “Tell them the calm has been discontinued.”

Cassian's mouth tightened. “If I answer, they will trace this chamber.”

“They already know where we are,” Ivo said. “The question is whether you will use the channel to order soldiers against people who have just learned why their families disappeared.”

For a moment Mara thought Cassian might do it. The old reflex passed visibly through him: command, conceal, contain. Then he pressed the channel open.

“This is Cassian Or,” he said. “The central synchronization is no longer under Directorate authority. All units are ordered to hold position. Do not fire on civilians. Do not seal clinics or reservoirs. Await local instructions.”

The reply came at once. “Minister Or, you are compromised. Repeat the stability directive.”

Cassian looked at Mara. She could see the question in his eyes, and also the shame of having to ask it.

“Say what is true,” she told him.

He faced the microphone. “The Directorate's stability directive is void.”

The channel shrieked and cut out.

Then every light on the command band went black.

Across the city, preparation began to matter more than courage.

At the ferry depot school, Eli had been painting a wall when the first wave of remembered images came through. He did not see them as a single story. He saw a red cup tipping across a metal table, a row of people in raincoats, a boy with one shoe, and his sister's voice saying a phrase he could not place. Nia found him sitting beneath the mural with both hands pressed to his ears.

“Do you know me?” she asked.

Eli lowered one hand. “I know your cloth.”

The faded red strip was tied around Nia's wrist. She touched it, then touched his paint-spattered sleeve.

“I know your blue,” she said.

It was not an answer, but it was enough. Teacher Sella knelt beside them and placed a slate between their bodies. On it she wrote: WHAT I REMEMBER. WHAT I THINK. WHAT I DO NOT KNOW.

Around the room, children and adults copied the headings. One woman insisted that her father had been taken from a hospital in Year Three. A man across from her said the same father had died in a storm. Sella did not choose between them. She wrote both accounts and asked who had witnessed each one.

When a man began shouting that the Directorate had stolen his whole childhood, two older students guided him toward the quiet room. No one told him to stop grieving. No one told him that grief proved the archive was correct.

Eli rose, picked up his brush, and added a small open door to the mural. Beneath it he painted a line of names. Some he knew. Some he marked with a circle.

“Why the circles?” Nia asked.

“Because a name can be true even when I don't know what happened to the person.”

At the South Belt clinic, Anja's instructions had become a kind of liturgy. Drink water. Lower the noise. Ask permission before touching. Check medication timing. Separate a seizure from panic, panic from grief, grief from a harbor fault. Record what happened without turning it into a permanent identity.

The clinics had prepared for hundreds. They received thousands.

Some patients collapsed when suppressed memories returned. Others remembered nothing and suffered because everyone around them suddenly expected a revelation. A few laughed uncontrollably. One former Guardian sat beneath a table for three hours, whispering the names of children he had escorted into correction rooms. A medic found him there and asked whether he wanted treatment. He said yes. She treated him without asking whether he deserved it.

In the neighboring assembly hall, food counters opened. The upper reservoir residents sent down pipes and portable tanks. At first they came under escort, afraid that lower-district families would tear them apart. Instead, the council made them sign the same public inventory as everyone else.

“Your names go on the ledger,” Tomas told a reservoir keeper who had once denied water access to three raft communities. “Not because we forgive you. Because hidden valves made this possible, and we are done with hidden things.”

The keeper looked toward the crowd. “What happens to us?”

“Today? You unload water.”

“And tomorrow?”

“Tomorrow you answer questions.”

The answer disappointed those who wanted punishment and frightened those who expected it. That was, Mara thought, a beginning.

By evening, technicians were working district by district. They gathered around old harbor junctions with Sera's diagrams copied on ceramic, the medical confirmation forms Anja had laminated, and witnesses who understood neither the code nor the politics but could attest to what had been done.

No one pulled a master lever.

At Lantern Quays, a technician named Oren removed the obedience protocol from labor eligibility while a clinic nurse watched the seizure monitors. At South Belt, another team paused twice because a medication schedule failed to match the archive. At the raft moorings, residents refused the change until an independent mechanic found a cracked relay housing.

Each correction traveled back to the central archive. Each failure remained visible.

Mara heard the reports through the night.

“District Seven separation complete. Medical lattice stable.”

“District Nine paused. One unexplained tremor in the pediatric channel.”

“District Eleven refusing authorization until two more witnesses arrive.”

“Record the refusal,” Mara said every time. “A refusal is not sabotage.”

The city did not become free in a single clean motion. It became less commanded. That was messier.

Near midnight, a squad of soldiers arrived at the relay entrance. Their weapons were lowered, but Tomas moved in front of the door anyway.

The youngest soldier removed his helmet. “We were ordered to secure the chamber.”

“By whom?” Tomas asked.

The soldier held out a dead command band. “No one now.”

Behind him, two others were crying. One carried a photograph copied from the archive: a family on a roof, the water already at their knees. The Directorate record had called them displaced casualties. The photograph had names written on the back.

“Our unit was assigned to clear the western evacuation route,” the soldier said. “We were told there were no civilians left.”

Mara stepped toward him. “You can put down your weapon and enter without one. Or you can leave. No one here will make you join us.”

He looked at the armed volunteers behind her. “What are you going to do with officers?”

“Protect them from a crowd,” Mara said. “Then place them before a witnessed council, with records and the right to answer.”

Tomas's face hardened. “Some answers will not be enough.”

“No,” Mara said. “But we will not build the next system by deciding that one person's anger is a court.”

The soldier set his rifle on the floor.

By dawn, three more units had abandoned their posts. Some walked away toward their families. Some came to the assembly halls. Some stayed at the water stations because they knew how to operate the pumps. The city learned that refusing an order did not automatically make a person wise or good. It only made a new choice possible.

Cassian was gone.

Mara found the empty command alcove after the morning shift. His coat was still hanging beside the column. On the floor lay his dead command band and a small paper photograph, softened by years of handling. His daughter stood in shallow floodwater beside a yellow buoy, her face turned away from the camera.

Pell checked the maintenance records. “He left through the east service passage at 04:17.”

“Alone?”

“According to the pressure plate.”

Tomas swore. “He is running.”

“Or remembering,” Anja said. “Those are not mutually exclusive.”

A search party formed before anyone could authorize it. Dockworkers took hooks and lamps. Two young activists wanted to drag Cassian back publicly. A former Guardian offered to lead them through the submerged ruins beneath the old city, where the old command passages connected to the drowned transit lines.

Mara stopped them at the hatch.

“You will search for him,” she said, “but you will not hunt him.”

“He commanded the correction rooms,” one activist said.

“And that will be recorded. His testimony will not erase the harm, and his disappearance will not erase it either.” Mara looked at the weapons, the hooks, the faces bright with exhaustion and certainty. “Bring him back alive if he is alive. Bring back evidence if he is not. No killing in the name of the archive.”

Tomas stepped close. “You are protecting him.”

“I am protecting what we said the archive was for.”

He held her gaze for a long time. Then he lowered his hook.

The searchers entered the ruins under a white witness lamp. They found Cassian's footprints where the passage descended below the tide line, and one of his gloves caught on a broken stair. Beyond that, only black water and the distant knocking of loose metal.

At the central relay, Mara returned to the consoles. She had not slept. Ivo draped his patched coat around her shoulders and leaned against the panel, his bad leg trembling.

“Food,” he said.

“After District Four confirms its clinic.”

“Food before District Four.”

She looked at him, then at the list in her hand. “You sound like Anja.”

“I am becoming unbearable with age.”

“You are thirty-two.”

“Ancient. Feed me.”

She smiled despite herself. The smile hurt, but not in a way she wanted removed.

Outside, New Carthage made noise. Not the synchronized hum of a city obeying one pulse, but the irregular sounds of work: valves turning, children arguing, pumps restarting, bells calling people to meetings. Grief moved through the harbors like weather. So did anger. So did the uncertain labor of care.

Mara placed her hand on the relay's quiet casing.

No voice belonged to one person now. Not Sera's. Not Cassian's. Not hers.

“Open the next district channel,” she said.

Pell began turning the crank. Anja checked the clinic reports. Ivo unfolded the route ledger. Tomas went to the water crews.

And the harbors, one by one, opened.

set.name: Mara Venn
set.description: Mara is at the central relay beneath New Carthage after the broadcast, coordinating district clinics, archive channels, harbor technicians, water crews, and witnessed councils with Ivo, Anja, Tomas, and Pell. She is exhausted and sleep-deprived but emotionally steady, and has refused to claim personal victory or allow mob justice against former Directorate officials. She knows the archive has caused confusion, grief, neurological distress, and isolated violence, while preparation has prevented total collapse; she is committed to finishing district separations, preserving medical care, and keeping authority rotating and contestable. She carries her decision book, route ledgers, broadcast packets, archive copies, and technical instructions, and wears Ivo's patched coat while returning to work.

set.name: Eli Venn
set.description: Eli is at the ferry depot school with Nia, teachers, children, and support workers after the broadcast. He remains a public muralist and visual historian, using paint and the depot's quiet rooms to help people distinguish memory, belief, and uncertainty. He still recognizes Mara inconsistently by face but trusts her voice, habits, and chosen phrases; he is vulnerable to crowd noise and memory shocks but is contributing open-door and name imagery to the school's murals. Nia's faded red cloth remains part of the school's visual memory.

set.name: Ivo Renn
set.description: Ivo is at the central relay beside Mara, coordinating courier routes, school channels, clinic reports, water and energy manifests, and district communications after the broadcast. He and Mara remain in a loving relationship; he is physically tired, his limp is aggravated, and he insists that Mara eat and rest while continuing to help. He knows the archive has reached the city and that the decentralized network must finish the work without replacing Directorate control with movement control. His patched courier coat, route books, signal mirrors, waterproof lists, and copied technical materials remain with him.

set.name: Anja Quill
set.description: Anja is working between the central relay and the city clinics, directing treatment for seizures, panic, dissociation, grief, and harbor-related trauma while insisting these conditions be distinguished and documented. She has medical cases, stabilizers, medication lists, laminated instructions, consent forms, quiet-room plans, and clinic ledgers. She knows local councils are distributing food, water, and energy and that district separations have begun but still require pauses and technical correction. She remains precise, tired, and committed to care regardless of political agreement.

set.name: Tomas Vale
set.description: Tomas is moving between the central relay, water crews, and local councils after the broadcast. He helped secure opened reservoirs and continues organizing dockworkers, but has accepted Mara's insistence that disarmed former officials receive witnessed accountability rather than mob punishment. He remains angry at the Directorate and impatient with delay, while helping preserve pumps, food distribution, energy, and transport. He carries his work placard and dock tools and knows that district harbor separation and civic control are still incomplete.

set.name: Pell
set.description: Pell is at the central relay documenting the broadcast's aftermath with mechanical recorders, consent ledgers, technical packets, pause and refusal records, and public archive copies. She has recorded Cassian's final command-channel failure, the district separations begun, technical pauses, and the search for Cassian in the submerged ruins. She remains physically strained but focused on distinguishing access records, testimony, interpretation, and correction.

set.name: Cassian Or
set.description: Cassian Or lost effective control of the Directorate after the broadcast and publicly ordered units not to fire before declaring its stability directive void. Emotionally shaken by unedited records of his daughter's death and politically isolated, he left the central relay alone through an east service passage into the submerged ruins. His command band and photograph remain at the relay; searchers found his trail and a glove but do not know whether he is alive. He remains subject to future witnessed testimony and accountability rather than mob justice.

set.name: Nia
set.description: Nia is at the ferry depot school with Eli, teachers, and support workers after experiencing the broadcast's wave of memories. She remains emotionally vulnerable but supported by quiet rooms and familiar people, and continues learning visual history while wearing the faded red family cloth around her wrist. She and Eli rely on tangible colors, objects, and chosen phrases when faces and family memories feel uncertain.

The civic network prevented citywide collapse after the broadcast: teachers opened testimony rooms, clinics treated harbor-related distress, and local councils distributed food, water, and energy while honoring district pauses.
Upper-district residents opened private reservoirs, and public inventories made the newly shared water supplies visible to lower-district councils.
Harbor technicians began removing obedience protocols district by district while preserving medical functions, recording pauses, refusals, and technical failures in public ledgers.

Dockworkers refused military orders, several soldiers abandoned their posts after receiving unedited family memories, and Mara established that disarmed former officers would receive witnessed accountability rather than mob justice.
Cassian lost effective control of the Directorate and entered the submerged ruins alone; searchers found his trail but did not determine whether he survived.
The decentralized councils must finish the remaining district harbor separations, investigate technical failures, and preserve public copies of every change before the new civic system is secure.

The councils must continue the witnessed accountability process for former Directorate officials, including locating Cassian Or if he survived the submerged ruins and preserving his testimony without coercion.

chapters.name: Nothing Belongs to One Voice
chapters.content:
The first rule of the archive was painted above the door in three languages and one stubborn child’s handwriting:

NO RECORD IS ABOVE QUESTION.

The child had made the letters too tall. The last word slanted upward as if question itself were a hill. Mara had left it that way.

Below the sign, the old ferry depot had become the House of Many Hands. Its roof still carried the scars of the storm that had opened the correction facility years ago, but wind turbines now turned along the ridge, and rain collectors shone like a row of silver bowls. People came through the doors carrying notebooks, cracked harbor plates, family photographs, fishing permits, ration complaints, and memories they did not know how to name.

Mara stood at the public desk with her daughter asleep against her shoulder.

“Your turn,” said Olan, the morning clerk. “The South Belt has sent a challenge to the reservoir figures.”

“Of course they have.”

“They say the upper reservoirs are being counted as communal but managed as private.”

“They are right to challenge it.”

Olan smiled. “I hoped you would say that. The assembly treasurer hoped you would say something more encouraging.”

Mara shifted the child, who made a small, indignant noise and burrowed into the patched fold of her coat. “Encouragement is not an archival category.”

“It should be. Half the city is trying to govern while sleep deprived.”

“Then record that accurately.”

He made a note. In the public ledger, every amendment retained its earlier form beneath the new one. No hand could erase a mistake; no official could make a correction look like an original certainty. It made the books thick, slow, and honest enough to be inconvenient.

That was the point.

Mara opened the reservoir file. The figures had been copied from three district ledgers, one water crew’s mechanical tally, and a private upper-district account. The accounts disagreed by six thousand liters. Six thousand liters could be a calculation error. It could also be six thousand people receiving one less cup a day.

“Call a water witness from Lantern Quays,” she said. “And someone from the upper cistern crews. Not the treasurer.”

“Someone who disagrees with the treasurer?”

“Someone who has touched the valves.”

The child woke. Her name was Jun, and at five years old she had perfected the art of appearing alert whenever her mother began an argument. She lifted her head and surveyed the room with Mara’s dark, solemn eyes.

“Are we fighting?” Jun asked.

“Not yet,” Mara said.

“Will there be fighting?”

“There will be a meeting.”

Jun considered this. “That means yes, but with chairs.”

Olan laughed. Mara tried not to, and failed.

At the far wall, a group of schoolchildren were studying a mural. Eli had painted it over three winters: a drowned street beneath layered waves, a red cup tipped on its side, seven marks around an open door, and hundreds of names rising like plankton through the water. Some names were certain. Some were followed by a question mark. One section was blank except for the words WE ARE STILL LOOKING.

Eli stood before the mural with a pointer in his hand.

“Do not call this a picture of what happened,” he told the children. “Call it a picture of what people remembered, recorded, argued about, and changed.”

A boy in a yellow maintenance vest raised his hand. “But which part is true?”

“Which part do you mean?”

“The red cup.”

Eli glanced at it. His face had grown leaner over the years, his hair threaded with copper where Mara remembered it being entirely dark. He still sometimes failed to recognize her by sight. He knew her by voice, by the way she tapped a spoon twice against a bowl, by the phrase she used when she was frightened and pretending not to be: We can begin with what we have.

“The cup is true as a remembered image,” he said. “It may not be true as proof of where it was, or whose hand knocked it over. Mara wrote that distinction beside the first drawing. I kept it.”

“Why keep something that might be wrong?” asked a girl.

“Because wrong things can teach us how we became certain.”

The children grew quiet. Beyond the windows, ferries moved between the districts, their hulls painted with the colors of the federated assembly: no single color allowed to cover the others.

Eli saw Mara and lifted the pointer in greeting. Jun waved both hands.

“Your daughter has been correcting my dates,” Eli said when the lesson ended.

“She has inherited the family vice.”

“Questioning?”

“Interrupting.”

Jun pointed at the mural. “Uncle Eli says the Directorate did bad things, but the Rememberers did bad things too.”

“Some Rememberers did,” Mara said. “Some officials did. Some people did brave things and harmful things on the same day.”

Jun frowned. “That is too many things.”

“Yes.” Mara kissed the crown of her head. “History is often inconveniently crowded.”

They walked after midday to the Assembly House, which had once been a Directorate customs hall. Its statues had been removed, but their empty plinths remained. On each stood a rotating display: a water valve, a school slate, a clinic ledger, a broken drone, a child’s red cloth. The objects changed every month, chosen by districts that did not get to choose again until all the others had.

Ivo was waiting beneath the stairwell, arguing with two repair cooperatives and a teacher from the North Floats. He wore a new coat now, though the patched courier jacket hung from his shoulders like a second skin whenever work became urgent. His limp was still visible in cold weather. Today he leaned on a brass-handled tool, not because he needed it, but because he had forgotten to put it down.

“The school roofs cannot wait for the next allocation cycle,” said the teacher.

“The repair crews cannot manufacture slate from promises,” said a cooperatives’ delegate.

“Then put the shortage in the record,” Ivo said. “Ask the children to sit beneath it until the assembly becomes ashamed.”

“That is not a repair method,” Mara said.

“It has an excellent success rate.”

He kissed her temple, then took Jun from her arms with a grunt when the child immediately demanded to be carried higher.

“You’re late,” he said.

“I was verifying water theft.”

“Alleged water miscount.”

“Your phrasing is why I married you.”

“I thought it was my heroic limp.”

“Among other defects.”

They joined the afternoon session. The federated assembly did not resemble the old Directorate’s tower, where decisions had descended polished and complete. Here, every delegation brought unfinished proposals. Lower-district councils argued with upper-district councils about reservoirs, schools, ferry access, and the lingering distribution of repair metals. Old families still had better rooms and better tools. Old prejudices survived in gentler language. People who had once obeyed the Directorate sometimes demanded a central authority again, claiming that debate was a luxury of the fed.

A man from the Heights stood to speak.

“My parents remember when a single office could settle a question in an hour,” he said. “Now it takes six meetings to decide where to put a pump.”

“Your parents also remember who was allowed to drink from it,” called someone from the South Belt.

The hall tightened.

Mara rose before the exchange became a contest of inherited wounds. “Both records belong in the room,” she said. “The speed may have been real. So was the exclusion. We are not required to choose which fact makes the better slogan.”

The man from the Heights looked at her with open irritation. “You always make everything more complicated.”

“Water already is.”

That won a few laughs, but not agreement. The assembly continued until the proposal was divided into two questions: immediate repairs, and a public review of reservoir management. Neither question was solved. Both were scheduled, witnessed, and assigned names.

At dusk, Mara took Jun home through the western market. A vendor was selling printed portraits of the first assembly delegates. Cassian Or was not among them. His disappearance remained an absence in every official record: an unresolved flight into the submerged ruins, followed by years of testimony from those who had served under him. Some wanted a symbolic trial without a body. Others wanted to declare him dead and close the matter. The accountability council had refused both shortcuts.

Mara had once thought justice meant finding the correct ending. Now she understood that a process could be an act of memory too. No one could be allowed to disappear into a convenient story—not Cassian, not Sera, not the people whose names survived only as uncertain marks.

At home, Ivo prepared supper while Jun arranged wooden valves into a city on the floor. Mara opened the day’s archive packet. There were three complaints, two corrections, one accusation of favoritism, and a letter from a school asking permission to reproduce the original broadcast in lessons for older children.

She read the letter twice.

“Are you going to say yes?” Ivo asked.

“Yes, with conditions. Medical warnings, quiet rooms, context, and no treating the broadcast as sacred.”

“Good.” He set a bowl before her. “You should eat before you democratize anything else.”

After supper, Mara and Jun walked to the neighborhood memory house. Children were already gathered around a low table, where a teacher had placed copies of three documents: the Directorate’s final synchronization order, the Rememberers’ early emergency bulletin, and the first assembly’s resource plan.

The teacher asked, “What did each group get wrong?”

A child pointed to the Directorate order. “They thought control was safety.”

Another pointed to the Rememberer bulletin. “They thought being right meant being ready.”

A third studied the assembly plan. “They thought writing a rule meant people would follow it.”

Mara stood in the doorway, listening.

On the wall hung Sera’s ceramic plate, not as a relic above the children but at their eye level beside a label: ENGINEERING INSTRUCTION, PARTIAL SURVIVAL, SOURCE AND LIMITS RECORDED. Beneath it, someone had added a fresh card.

WHAT WOULD YOU CHANGE?

Jun took Mara’s hand. “Did Grandmother save the city?”

Mara looked at the plate. For years she had wanted Sera to be innocent, then brave, then alive long enough to see what followed. The wanting had not vanished. It had simply stopped being the only truth available.

“She helped make a tool,” Mara said. “She helped us understand how it was used. Other people carried the understanding farther than she could.”

“Did you save it?”

“No.”

Jun looked disappointed.

Mara knelt so they were level. “I helped. So did Ivo. So did Uncle Eli. So did Anja, Tomas, Pell, the water crews, the children who opened doors, the people who kept records, and the people who argued with records until they improved. No one saved it alone.”

Jun examined the room, the cards, the listening children. “Then who owns the story?”

Mara heard the old harbor hum beneath the floor. It was no longer a command disguised as comfort. It was a medical lattice, monitored by many hands, interruptible by anyone who could show cause. The city still groaned, still failed, still had to be repaired.

“No one,” she said. “That is why we have to keep telling it.”

At the archive the next morning, Mara would sign the reservoir correction. Ivo would visit three schools and a roof crew. Eli would add a blank space to the mural for a name not yet confirmed. Jun would ask another impossible question.

The world had changed, but not into certainty. It had changed into a practice: preserve what happened, question what was claimed, care for those harmed by knowing, and act together before the next disaster made a lesson of them.

Above the House of Many Hands, the crooked sign lifted in the wind.

NO RECORD IS ABOVE QUESTION.

The letters held.

Not because one voice had painted them, but because many hands had refused to let them be erased.

set.name: Mara Venn
set.description: Mara lives in New Carthage with Ivo and their five-year-old daughter Jun. She is an elected archivist at the House of Many Hands and helps the federated civic assembly preserve public records, investigate contested resource figures, and teach children to distinguish testimony, evidence, uncertainty, and correction. She knows the city's harbor obedience protocols have been separated from medical protections, though the new society remains unequal and politically contested. She remains committed to rotating, contestable authority and rejects personal ownership of the revolution or its story. She carries archive packets, public ledgers, correction records, and the habits learned from Sera's instructions; she is tired but emotionally grounded and continues to care for family, civic memory, and practical repair.

set.name: Eli Venn
set.description: Eli lives and works in New Carthage as a teacher of visual history and public muralist. He uses murals to preserve erased names, distinguish certain from uncertain memories, and teach children how testimony and interpretation differ. He still sometimes fails to recognize Mara by sight but knows her voice, habits, and chosen phrases; their relationship is affectionate and trusted. He keeps the red-cup, seven-marked door, open-door, and connected-circle imagery in the city's visual history while leaving spaces for unresolved identities. He is emotionally steadier but remains attentive to memory uncertainty and crowd-related strain.

set.name: Ivo Renn
set.description: Ivo lives with Mara and their daughter Jun in New Carthage. He coordinates schools, repair cooperatives, ferry links, and practical allocations within the federated civic network. He and Mara remain loving partners and share parenting, political disagreement, and work. His old limp is visible in cold weather, but he remains active and carries a brass-handled repair tool as well as route and allocation knowledge. He knows that debate is slower than Directorate command but safer and more inclusive, and he works to keep schools and infrastructure functioning despite contested resources and persistent inequality.

set.name: Sera Venn
set.description: Sera remains missing and likely dead after Directorate capture. Her ceramic separation plate and final technical instructions are preserved publicly at the House of Many Hands with their source, limits, and partial survival recorded. Her legacy is treated as engineering, warning, and contribution rather than private property or sainthood; Mara continues to remember her with love while teaching that other people carried Sera's understanding forward.

set.name: Dagan Pell
set.description: Dagan Pell's present location and condition remain unknown. His forbidden founding-song verses and hand-copied names list are part of the community memory preserved by the public archive, though Mara continues to distinguish the surviving record from certainty about his fate.

set.name: Anja Quill
set.description: Anja works within the decentralized civic medical and archival system, whose clinics and public records remain active after harbor separation. Her methods of documenting symptoms, consent, uncertainty, and corrections continue to shape civic archives and education. She remains a trusted elder of the network, committed to care and skeptical of simplified historical claims.

set.name: Tomas Vale
set.description: Tomas remains associated with dockworkers, water crews, and civic resource organization. His movement from sabotage toward strikes and essential-infrastructure protection helped establish the current system, though anger at former Directorate power and impatience with slow procedures persist among workers and in him. His work and arguments remain part of the public record rather than being converted into a heroic legend.

set.name: Pell
set.description: Pell remains a public-record keeper within the civic archive network, preserving original recordings, permissions, corrections, technical records, and uncertainty. She helped establish standards that prevent any central archive or authority from secretly altering the past. Her exact current post is rotating among archive and assembly sites, and she remains physically strained but dedicated to transparent documentation.

set.name: Cassian Or
set.description: Cassian Or remains missing in the submerged ruins, with no confirmed evidence of death or survival. His command band and photograph remain archived, and the witnessed accountability council refuses both a symbolic trial without him and a convenient declaration of death. Former Directorate officials are subject to non-coercive testimony and public review rather than mob justice, and Cassian's unresolved status remains a civic obligation.

set.name: Nia
set.description: Nia is now part of the post-Directorate civic education community and remains connected to the ferry-depot school and its quiet-room practices. Her faded red family cloth continues to appear in the school's visual history. She and other formerly conditioned children are represented as witnesses with care needs and uncertainty, not as political symbols whose memories can be claimed by an institution.

Several years after the broadcast, New Carthage completed its district harbor separations and was governed by a federated civic assembly whose public archives preserved originals, corrections, uncertainty, and dissent.
Mara became an elected archivist and mother, Ivo coordinated schools and repair cooperatives, and Eli taught visual history through murals that marked uncertain names and memories.
The new civic system publicly taught the catastrophe, the Directorate's crimes, the Rememberers' mistakes, and the assembly's failures rather than treating any account as sacred or final.
The federated assembly must resolve the contested six-thousand-liter reservoir discrepancy through witnessed water-valve audits and a public review of upper-district reservoir management.

errors.quote: Mara looked around the room. At thirty, she was tired enough to understand that a promise was heavier than a speech.

errors.pair: He looked older than sixteen in the weak blue light, which made Mara angry at the Directorate, at Dagan, at the list beneath her shirt, and finally at herself for having no one to blame who could be reached.
